numeral|)
summary: Numerals in Kalamang are a subclass of quantifiers with three special diagnostics: they can be reduplicated to mark distributive meaning, take classifier prefixes, and combine with the suffix -gan ‘all’. Reduplicated numerals can function attributively or predicatively, classifier + numeral forms follow the noun directly, and -gan is used with numerals such as eir ‘two’ to mean ‘both’, but it cannot attach to nouns, which require a different quantifier for meanings like ‘all houses’.

text:
Kalamang has six non-numeral quantifiers, listed in Table tab:quant. For some comments on their individual properties, see § sec:quantall. Unlike numeral classifiers, these cannot be reduplicated to create a distributive distributive quantifier and they cannot be preceded by a classifier.

quantifier|)
summary: Kalamang has six non-numeral quantifiers. Unlike numeral classifiers, these quantifiers cannot be reduplicated to form distributive quantifiers and cannot be preceded by a classifier.

text:
demonstrative|(

Demonstratives form a closed class of words that locate a referent in space, time or discourse in relation to the deictic centre. Pronominally, demonstratives take the slot of the noun; identificationally, demonstratives occur in copula copula*!clause and non-verbal clauses; adnominally, demonstratives occur after the noun. There are six demonstratives, which behave differently with respect to their ability to occur in these slots. Table tab:demwc gives an overview of the demonstrative roots and their syntactic use. There are five demonstrative roots whose main function is to locate a referent in space in relation to the deictic centre. Wa is generally associated with proximal reference, and me with more distal reference. These may occur pronominally, adnominally and identificationally. A third deictic demonstrative root, far distal owa, only occurs adnominally and identificationally, and occurs much less frequently than wa and me. demonstrative!elevational Elevationals yawe ` down ' and osa ` up ' occur adnominally and identificationally. In addition, there is an anaphoric demonstrative, opa, which is only used adnominally. The description of demonstratives is expanded upon in Chapter ch:dems.

The same root is used in all positions, as illustrated below for proximal wa. Wa and me as adnominal and pronominal demonstratives are infrequent; almost all corpus occurrences of wa and me are identificational. The three uses are illustrated in ( exe:demad ) (adnominal), ( exe:demad2 ) (pronominal), ( exe:demid ) (identificational in argument function) and ( exe:demidpred ) (identificational in predicate function). When used adnominally or identificationally in argument function, the demonstrative is almost invariably followed by me ` '.

goras wa me bara=te kul nerunggo sor=at jie\\
crow prox descend= basket inside fish= obj get\\
`This crow went down into the basket and got a fish.' [stim3_0:05]

ma wat paruo\\
3sg prox.obj make\\
`She made this.' [conv17_8:37]

wa me yartep\\
prox sardine\\
`This is a sardine.' [stim15_2:03]

namun=a wa kiun=a wa tumun-un=a wa \\
husband.3poss=foc prox wife.3poss=foc prox child -3poss=foc prox \\
`Her husband is this, his wife is this, their child is this.' [stim6_19:23]

exe

The demonstrative!elevational elevationals yawe ` down ' and osa ` up ' can only be used adnominally and identificationally. This is illustrated for yawe ` down ' in ( exe:yawekom ) (adnominal) and ( exe:lempyawe ) (identificational).

exe

ma tama ka bo minggalot-an yawe komere\\
3sg where 2sg go bedroom- 1sg.poss down look\\
`Where is it? You go look in my bedroom down there.' [conv17_3:42]

lempuang yawe \\
island down \\
`The island is down there.' [stim43_2:22]

exe

The demonstrative roots wa, me, owa, yawe and osa can take the lative enclitic =ka and the locative =ko (§ sec:demcase ). The roots wa and me are also used to create manner, quality, quantity and degree demonstratives (§ sec:mqqd ).

Finally, there is a demonstrative opa, which is always used adnominally. It signals that a referent represents shared knowledge between the speaker and addressee. This demonstrative is further described in § sec:demopa and. An example is given in ( exe:udangopa ).

exe
udang opa ka kuet=nin\\
lobster 2sg get= neg \\
`Didn't you get that lobster (we talked about earlier)?' [conv1_6:05]

demonstrative|)
summary: Demonstratives are a closed class used to locate referents in space, time, or discourse relative to the deictic center, and they can function pronominally, identificationally, or adnominally depending on position. The language has six demonstratives with different distribution: wa and me are the main spatial deictics and can occur in all three functions, owa is farther distal and only adnominal/identificational, yawe and osa are elevational forms used adnominally and identificationally, and opa is always adnominal and marks shared knowledge. The roots wa, me, owa, yawe, and osa can also take lative and locative enclitics, and wa and me additionally form manner, quality, quantity, and degree demonstratives.

text: Postpositions These are analysed as postpositions, not case markers, because of the domain of attachment (the NP, not the noun), a lack of agreement or declension paradigms, and because the forms are almost mutually exclusive. The author has no strong preference for either analysis, and encourages the reader to replace ``postposition'' with ``case marker'' in their mind if they wish. postposition mark the function of core and peripheral argument noun phrases. argument!core argument!peripheral Kalamang has nine postpositions: object =at, comitative =bon, instrumental =ki, benefactive =ki, similative =kap, locative =ko, animate locative =konggo, lative =ka and animate lative =kongga. They are enclitics that attach to the right edge of the NP. noun phrase The postpositions are further described in Chapter ch:noun. References to the specific sections are given in Table tab:wcpos.
summary: The passage says that Kalamang’s nine postpositions are analyzed as postpositions rather than case markers because they attach to the whole noun phrase, do not show agreement or declension, and are mostly mutually exclusive. However, the author notes there is no strong preference between the two analyses and suggests readers may think of them as case markers if they prefer. These enclitic forms mark core and peripheral argument noun phrases, attaching to the right edge of the NP.

text:
modifier!adverbial

Adverbial modifiers is a cover term for morphemes that modify the clause by changing the mood, aspect or mode of a predicate or clause; or specify the manner, temporal setting, degree or other characteristics of the state or event expressed by the verb, such as repetition repetition or exclusivity. They are independent words, proclitics, enclitics and suffixes that occupy different slots in the clause. They do not form a real word class, but are given here for ease of reference. Adverbial modifiers can be divided into functional groups such as modal adverbials or manner adverbials. See Chapter ch:clausmod for an overview of all morphemes and their positions in the clause. One important position is the post-subject position, which is taken by iamitive iamitive se, nondum nondum tok, See and for a definition of and information about the categories iamitive and nondum, respectively. gen `maybe' and some modal adverbials. The predicate can host a number of clitics, including mood and aspect markers. Clausal negation is also marked as a clitic on the predicate (described in § sec:clauneg ).

The following examples illustrate post-subject iamitive se and koi `again' in ( exe:hekoi ), clause-final reon `maybe' in ( exe:gongreon ), clause-initial temporal adverbials and progressive =teba and volitional =kin on the predicate in ( exe:kasurm ).

exe

mu se koi yal\\
3pl again paddle\\
`They already paddled again.' [narr19_10:06]

esa anggon temun=a an=at gonggung reon \\
father 1sg.poss big= foc 1sg=obj call maybe\\
`Maybe my uncle called me.' [conv9_9:20]

ma toni opa_yuwa an dodon waruo= teba kasur mu kolak=ka bot= kin \\
3sg say today 1sg clothes wash= tomorrow 3pl mountain= lat go= \\
`She said: ``Today I'm washing clothes.'' Tomorrow they want to go to the mountains.' [conv11_6:15]

exe
summary: Adverbial modifiers are a broad cover term for morphemes that modify a clause by changing mood, aspect, mode, or by indicating manner, time, degree, repetition, exclusivity, and similar meanings. They are not a single word class, but include independent words, proclitics, enclitics, and suffixes that occupy different clause positions; some examples are post-subject items like *se* and *nondum*, clause-final *maybe*, and clitics on the predicate such as mood, aspect, and negation markers.

text:
question word|(

Question words or content interrogatives are words that are used to make non-polar questions, indicating the part of the proposition that the speaker is asking about. They form a closed class. Question words take the slot of the constituent that the speaker is asking about. They cut across several word classes, with Kalamang having nominal, adnominal, predicative and adverbial question words, and one quantifier question word. Their main shared feature is that they structurally replace other constituents, which is why they are discussed together here. As for their form, all question words but neba `what' contain a sequence ama, and all but neba and naman `who' contain the sequence tama or its allophonic variant rama. The question words are listed in Table tab:wcques. Neba `what' is a very generic question word which can question both items and actions. It also functions as a placeholder placeholder for any constituent, see § sec:ph. wh-question|see question-word question interrogative placeholder question word question

Naman `who' and neba `what' are nominal, taking the place of subjects and objects in situ, with the ability to carry postpositions postposition (§ sec:wcnoun ). Naman replaces pronouns, being unable to carry possessive morphology, but having the possibility to carry generic possessive =kin or animate lative and locative postpositions =kongga and =konggo, respectively. Naman and neba, as well as tama below, can be followed by a focus focus marker =ba. In question-answer pairs, the answer may then also be followed by =ba, as in ( exe:namanba ).

exe

xlist
A:
naman =ba\\
who= \\
`Who?'

B:
an=ba\\
1sg = \\
`Me.' [overheard]

xlist

exe

exe
mena mu neba =at=a paruot=kin\\
then 3pl what= obj=foc do= \\
`Then, what do they want to do?' [narr45_3:01]

exe

Tama `which' usually modifies the noun in the NP, replacing a demonstrative. Neba does not occur replacing demonstratives.

exe

xlist
A:
anggas=at tarat-un eranun\\
door= obj close- nmlz cannot\\
`Couldn't you close the door?'

B:
anggas tama \\
door which\\
`Which door?' [conv9_17:05]

xlist

exe

Tamangga `to/from where' and tamatko `where' are formed with tama plus the lative or the locative enclitic, respectively (for the morphosyntax see § sec:problems ). They have verbal properties. Tamangga, like other words carrying lative =ka, is primarily used in predicate!complex complex predicates (see Chapter ch:svc ), for example with jie `get' in ( exe:tamjie ). Tamatko, like other words carrying locative =ko, is usually in predicate function. It can stand on its own, as illustrated in ( exe:tamatko ), or be accompanied by another verb. A short form of tamatko is tama. These suffixes are also described in § sec:lat and sec:loc. question word location

exe

ka tamangga =ta jie\\
2sg from_where= get\\
`Where did you get [it] from?' [conv1_5:23]

ema tamatko \\
mother where\\
`Where is mother?' [narr40_5:19]

exe

Tamandi is an adverbial question word. It is illustrated modifying komele `burn' in ( exe:qadv ), and paruo `do' in ( exe:babut ) below. In addition, it is used as a greeting greeting with the meaning `how are you doing?'. It seems to contain the suffix -ndi, which is also found on manner demonstratives (§ sec:mqqd ).

exe

din saerak in tamandi =a lampur=at komele\\
fire neg_exist 1pl.excl how= foc lamp= obj burn\\
`There was no fire, how could we burn the lamps?' [narr40_0:33]

exe

Puraman `how many' replaces a quantifier. ( exe:pel ) illustrates puraman following a classifier (§ sec:clf ).

exe

wat nak - puraman-i mindi kajie\\
coconut clf_fruit1 -how_many- objqnt like_that pick\\
`How many coconuts did [we] pick like that?' [conv11_4:50]

exe

Note that there is no question word for time. Yuol tama `which day' was elicited, but does not occur in the natural speech corpus. There is one occurrence of yuol puraman `which day'.

exe
ma toni yuol puraman usar=et\\
3sg say day how_many build_frame_house= \\
`Which day do [we] install the frame of the house?' [narr46_2:11]
exe

The syntax of questions with question words is further described in § sec:opq. question word|)
summary: Question words in Kalamang form a closed class used to ask non-polar questions by replacing the constituent under inquiry, and they span several word classes, including nominal, adnominal, predicative, adverbial, and quantifier forms. Most contain the sequences ama and tama/rama, with neba ‘what’ as a highly general placeholder, naman ‘who’ and neba functioning as nominal question words, and tama ‘which’ modifying nouns; there are also location-related forms tamangga and tamatko, the adverbial tamandi ‘how’, and puraman ‘how many’. The passage also notes that there is no dedicated question word for time.

text:
conjunction|(

Conjunctions are words that connect words, phrases or clauses. Kalamang has sequential, disjunctive, adversative, consequence and reason, concessive and conditional conjunctions. Coordination achieved with `and' in English is done by apposition apposition of two words, phrases or clauses in Kalamang, or, in the case of noun coordination, with comitative postposition postposition!comitative =bon (§ sec:comi ). Clause conjunction is described in depth in § sec:clauseconj. The three most common conjunctions are introduced here.

Ba `but' is an adversative coordinator conjunction!adversative, as illustrated in ( exe:babut ). It is also used to conjoin numerals numeral between 11 and 29, as described in § sec:cardnum.

exe

ma muawese ba ma tamandi paruot=et\\
3sg hungry but 3sg how do= \\
`He's hungry but what can he do?' [stim2_4:31]

exe

Ye `or' is a disjunctive coordinator conjunction!disjunctive. Intonationally, it belongs to the first clause. In addition to its coordinative function, it can also be used as a tag `maybe'. Both uses are illustrated in ( exe:ye ).

exe

Kalau sontum tur ye, don muat pue ye.\\
kalau sontum tur ye don mu=at pue ye\\
if person fall or thing 3pl=obj hit maybe\\
`If a person falls, or maybe a thing hits him...' [narr34_4:31]

exe

Eba `then' is used to connect two clauses that refer to sequential events conjunction!sequential. Intonationally, it belongs to the second clause. Koi `then' also expresses sequential meaning, but is often placed after the subject, although it can also be clause-initial when the subject is elided. There is no restriction on the combination of eba and koi. ( exe:eba ) illustrates post-subject koi and eba. ( exe:koicllnk ) illustrates koi clause-initially in an example where there is no subject because it is from a procedural text explaining how to build a traditional house. Koi is also an adverbial that means `again', see § sec:wcadv.

exe

In koi timunat potma, timunat potma bara melalu, eba in sensurgi kaborunat parair.\\
in koi timun=at potma timun=at potma bara melalu eba in sensur=ki kabor-un=at parair\\
1pl.excl then tip= obj cut tip= obj cut descend sit then 1pl.excl chainsaw= ins stomach- 3poss=obj chop\\
`Then we cut the tips, cut the tips and put [the canoe] down, then we chop its stomach with the chainsaw.' [narr14_1:39]

saban potmat=et koi kanggaran paruot=et\\
bamboo cut= then bamboo_floor make= \\
`[One] cuts bamboo, then [one] makes the bamboo floor.' [narr6_4:51]

exe

conjunction|)
summary:
Kalamang conjunctions link words, phrases, or clauses, and include sequential, disjunctive, adversative, consequence/reason, concessive, and conditional types. Coordination like English *and* is usually expressed by apposition, or by the comitative postposition *bon* in noun coordination.  

Among the common conjunctions described, *ba* means ‘but’ and can also join numerals from 11 to 29, *ye* means ‘or’ and can also function as a tag meaning ‘maybe’, and *eba* and *koi* express sequential ‘then’, with *koi* also able to mean ‘again’.

text:
interjection|(

Interjections are conventionalised utterances expressing spontaneous emotions or reactions. They are extra-grammatical and can be utterances on their own or they can be apposed to a sentence. They include cries of disgust or surprise, as well as greetings and words like `yes' and `no'.

Kalamang has a number of interjections that I have classified in a few semantic (and partly phonological) subcategories. These are listed here, together with their gloss used in the corpus, some words on their use and their phonological form. A non-exhaustive list of common interjections, their approximate form and their gloss is given in Table tab:inter. More information about the phonetics of Kalamang interjections can be found in § sec:int. They are further described and illustrated in § sec:discinterj.

Below I elaborate on the function of some of these interjections. filler

The remainder of interjections in the corpus that are not listed here are simply glossed as int, and include interjections of surprise like [oi] or [ui], calls like [ei], and a number of [o]'s indicating relief or recognition.

Conventions around greeting each other, asking for permission to leave, giving thanks and ending a narrative, among other things, are described in Chapter ch:inf. interjection|) word class|)
summary: Interjections are conventionalized utterances that express spontaneous emotions or reactions, and they are extra-grammatical, occurring either on their own or apposed to a sentence. In Kalamang, interjections are grouped into several semantic and partly phonological subcategories, with a non-exhaustive list of common forms given in a table and further discussion of their use and phonetics elsewhere in the grammar. Other corpus interjections are glossed simply as *int* and include expressions of surprise, calls, and sounds indicating relief or recognition.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
This chapter examines nouns in more detail. These were introduced in § sec:wcnoun as words that can be marked with possessive morphology. Here we also explore noun phrases (NPs), the larger units that are headed by nouns, and postpositional phrases (PPs), headed by postpositional enclitics to the NP.

The first two sections deal with nouns. Fundamental distinctions within the class of nouns are treated in § sec:nouncl and noun derivation in § sec:nomder. NP structure is described in § sec:nomphr, with sections on the different modifiers in the NP: quantifiers (§ sec:nmodqnt ), possessive pronouns (§ sec:nmodposs ), demonstratives (§ sec:nmoddem ), attributives (§ sec:attr ) and relative clauses (§ sec:relcla ). The fourth section (§ sec:case ) treats the marking of both core and peripheral arguments argument!peripheral, which are PPs headed by enclitic postpositions. NP coordination is treated in § sec:nomcord.

Chapters ch:pron to ch:dems describe in detail the main constituents of the NP other than the noun (pronouns, quantifiers, possessive markers and demonstratives).
summary:
This chapter expands on nouns, first reviewing their basic properties and internal distinctions, as well as noun derivation. It also describes noun phrases and their structure, including modifiers such as quantifiers, possessive pronouns, demonstratives, attributives, and relative clauses, and it treats case marking through postpositional phrases headed by enclitic postpositions.  

The chapter also covers NP coordination, while later chapters provide more detailed discussion of the main NP constituents other than nouns, including pronouns, quantifiers, possessive markers, and demonstratives.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun|(

Kalamang nouns can be divided into several subclasses. The first division is between proper nouns (§ sec:prop ) and common nouns (§ sec:comm ). Within the group of common nouns there are alienable and inalienable nouns (or free and bound roots) (§ sec:inal ). Mass nouns (§ sec:mass ) and some kinship terms (§ sec:kinnouns ) behave slightly differently from other nouns.
summary: Kalamang nouns are divided into proper nouns and common nouns. Common nouns are further split into alienable and inalienable nouns, and mass nouns and some kinship terms show slightly different behavior from other nouns.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
proper nouns

Proper nouns refer to unique places and (groups of) people. Proper nouns can be personal names names!personal names, family names, place names or ethnonyms. In contrast to common nouns, proper nouns cannot be reduplicated. Possessive suffixes (§ ch:poss ) on proper nouns are unattested in the corpus and only marginally accepted in elicitation. Proper nouns are not quantified. Otherwise, they behave similarly to common nouns, heading NPs. Person reference is described in § sec:nonpronref. Examples of place names names!place names can be found on the map of Karas on page ch:maps and in the dictionary dictionary dictionaria or the word list on page ch:wordlist.
summary: Proper nouns refer to unique places and groups of people, including personal names, family names, place names, and ethnonyms. Unlike common nouns, they cannot be reduplicated or quantified, and possessive suffixes on them are unattested in the corpus and only marginally accepted in elicitation. Otherwise, they behave like common nouns in that they head noun phrases.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text: Common nouns have a general reference to places, objects, persons, substances and abstract things. Unique reference to places and persons is the role of proper nouns (§ sec:prop ). The following subsections treat alienability distinctions, the behaviour of count and mass nouns and the behaviour of kinship terms.
summary: Common nouns refer generally to places, objects, persons, substances, and abstract things, while proper nouns have unique reference to places and persons. The following sections examine alienability distinctions, the behavior of count and mass nouns, and the behavior of kinship terms.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
alienability|(

Kalamang common nouns display an alienable/inalienable distinction. Alienable forms are free roots, which means they can always occur uninflected. The large majority of Kalamang nouns are alienable, and include words referring to places, objects, substances and abstract things, such as kolak `mountain; mainland', sasul `spoon', ror `tree; wood', ema `mother' and rer `story'. A small minority of the nouns are inalienable; they are bound roots that must carry a possessive suffix (Chapter ch:poss ).

Inalienable roots include certain kinship terms, part-of-whole terms and relational nouns. They can be divided into three groups based on the morphology they take and their semantic categories.

First, there is a small group of five roots A sixth root, teit- `neighbour', was elicited as inalienable but does not occur in the natural spoken corpus. which can never occur without a possessive suffix. They all refer to family members, and are listed in ( exe:fammembers ).

exe

xlist
dun- `opposite-sex sibling'
kia- `same-sex sibling; cousin'
kiar-/kie- `wife'
nam- `husband'
tara- `grandparent; grandchild'
xlist

exe

Other kinship kinship terms (see § sec:kinnouns and § sec:nonpronref ) are alienable, as are words like lidan `friend' and kiekter `shadow'. One kinship term, tumun `child', looks like it has the fossilised third-person possessive suffix -un, but is a free root. It has a reduplicated form tumtum `children', showing that the root is tum. Possessive suffixes, however, are attached to the root tumun: tumun-an `child- 1sg.poss ' and tumun-un `child- 3poss '.

Second, there is a larger group of inalienable nouns that specify parts of a whole part-of-whole. They almost always modify another noun, and tend to carry the third-person possessive marker -un. They typically refer to parts of plants or to ways of grouping units (e.g. poup- `bundle'). Table tab:pwhnouns contains the currently known examples from the corpus, but it is likely that more such forms exist. Forms marked with an asterisk are also classifiers, see § sec:clf.

Third, Kalamang has ten attested relational nouns noun!relational. These must be in a locative or lative NP (e.g. elak yumetko `bottom there' or elak=ka `to/from below'), or carry one of the following suffixes:

The relational location nouns are listed in Table tab:locationals. They are commonly inflected with the possessive suffix -un and sometimes also carry the locative postposition =ko. Some forms may directly carry =ko. Table tab:locationals shows the roots, the inflected forms and the forms with postpositions as they occur in the corpus.

( exe:siepsiep ) and ( exe:siun ) show siep- `edge' inflected with third-person possessive -un and with both -un and locative =ko. ( exe:kitko ), ( exe:kitpis ) and ( exe:kitkadok ) show kit- `top' with locative =ko, -pis `side' and -kadok `side'.

These suffixes, like locative =ko and lative =ka, are not exclusive to locational nouns. One example with predicative nouns -pis is given in ( exe:pis1 ).

A fourth group of bound roots related to noun categorisation are numeral classifiers. Though likely derived from nouns, they are not nouns themselves, but prefixes to numerals. There are fifteen classifiers, which occur in combination with a subset of the nouns. See § sec:clf for further discussion. alienability|)
summary: Kalamang common nouns show an alienable/inalienable contrast: most are alienable free roots, while a smaller set of inalienable nouns are bound roots that must take a possessive suffix. The inalienable nouns fall into several groups, including a small set of kinship terms, a larger set of part-of-whole nouns, and relational nouns that typically occur in locative or lative phrases and are often inflected with possessive or locative morphology. The passage also notes a separate set of numeral classifiers, which are bound forms used as prefixes to numerals rather than nouns.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
count noun|(

Within the group of common nouns, Kalamang has mass nouns and count nouns, which behave differently with respect to quantifiers (§ sec:wcquant ). Mass nouns require a measure noun when quantified with a numeral quantifier. This measure noun occurs between the noun and the quantifier. Examples of mass nouns are granular substances such as nasuena `sugar', os `sand', nd pasa `rice' and liquids such as per `water'. Examples of measure nouns are kiem `basket' and goni `sack'. Mass nouns can be quantified with most quantifiers, except taukon / ikon `a few', which is reserved for count nouns, as in ( exe:bob ). Their counterpart bolon `a little' is used for mass nouns, as in ( exe:nasbo ).

exe
tumtum taukon me Bobi emun=a kona\\
children few Bobi mother= foc see\\
`A few children, Bobi's mother saw [them].' [conv4_5:09]

nasuena bolon -i baran\\
sugar little- objqnt descend\\
`[You] put a little sugar in.' [conv11_1:55]

exe

Some nouns occur with classifiers when modified by a numeral numeral (§ sec:clf ). There is a difference between constructions with a mass noun combined with a measure noun on the one hand, and a (mass) noun with a classifier on the other hand. First, the use of classifiers is not obligatory in Kalamang, whereas the use of a mass noun directly followed by a numeral (without a measure noun) is ungrammatical. Second, measure nouns that can be used to quantify mass nouns can be used with any mass noun (the measure noun gelas `glass' can be used for any mass noun), and the measure noun chosen for a certain mass noun is not fixed (you can put tea in a glass, a mug, a thermos, a kettle, a hole in the ground, etc.). Classifiers can only be used with a specific subset of nouns. Third, measure nouns are alienable. Classifiers, on the other hand, are prefixes that attach to numeral quantifiers. count noun|)
summary:
Kalamang common nouns include both mass nouns and count nouns, which differ in how they combine with quantifiers. Mass nouns need a measure noun between the noun and numeral quantifier and cannot be directly followed by a numeral, while count nouns can take quantifiers like taukon/ikon ‘a few’; the contrasting form bolon ‘a little’ is used with mass nouns.

The passage also distinguishes measure nouns from classifiers. Measure nouns are optional, freely chosen, and can quantify any mass noun, whereas classifiers are not obligatory, apply only to a restricted set of nouns, and are prefixes attached to numeral quantifiers.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
kinship

Some kinship terms behave differently from other nouns, being the only nouns with a plural plural!nominal form. This is a collective plural, which means the plural forms refer to a group as a whole. All plurals are made with the suffix -mur or -mumur, which does not occur elsewhere in the language. imperative The imperative plural =r is described in § sec:imp. Kinship terms that have a plural form are listed in Table tab:mur. plural!nominal

Note that the singular terms for parallel cousins do not correspond completely. Dudanmur and kiamur are terms of reference for a person's cousins. The term of address (inflected for first-person singular) for a cousin of the same sex is kian `my sister/brother' and for a cousin of the opposite sex it is dunan `my sister/brother' (not dudan-an ). At the same time, there are no recorded plural forms for siblings. This means there is no overlap between the inalienable alienability kinship terms in § sec:inal and the kinship terms listed here. For more on kinship terms, see § sec:kinterms.
summary:
Some kinship terms are unusual in that they are the only nouns with a plural nominal form, and this plural is collective, referring to a group as a whole. These plurals are formed with the suffixes -mur or -mumur, which do not appear elsewhere in the language.  

The passage also notes that terms for parallel cousins differ between reference and address forms, and that no plural forms are recorded for siblings. As a result, there is no overlap between the inalienable kinship terms discussed elsewhere and the kinship terms listed here.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun derivation|(

Nouns can be derived in three ways. § sec:der discusses nouns derived from verbs. § sec:nounorig treats agentive nominalisation. § sec:nomcomp describes nominal compounds, which derive nouns from two nouns, or from a verb and a noun. Noun reduplication is described in § sec:nounredup.
summary: The passage says that nouns can be derived in three main ways: from verbs, through agentive nominalisation, and by nominal compounds formed from two nouns or from a verb and a noun. It also notes that noun reduplication is treated separately.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun derivation!verb-to-noun

A verb can be nominalised by the suffixing nominaliser -un (homonymous with third-person possessive marker -un ), such that it can assume the position of head of the NP. Derivation with -un happens in four contexts, presented here in order of frequency. First, verbs must be nominalised in combination with the verb eranun `cannot' (§ sec:lexicalneg ). Second, stative verbs can be nominalised to create attributive attribute nouns. Third, transitive verbs may be nominalised, which is especially common with Malay loans. Fourth, a kind of nominalisation takes place in verb pairs that are connected with the comitative postposition postposition!comitative =bon.

Verbs preceding eranun `cannot' must be nominalised with -un. A transitive example is given in ( exe:eranunnmlz ) and an intransitive one in ( exe:eranunintr ).

exe

anggas=at tarat-un eranun\\
door= obj close- nmlz cannot\\
`[He/she] cannot close the door.' [conv9_17:02]

ma toni o an nan-un eranun\\
3sg say emph 1sg consume- nmlz cannot\\
`He said: ``Oh, I cannot eat.''' [narr44_4:49]

exe

Attributive attribute!nominal nouns can be derived from intransitive stative verbs, such as kahenun `length; distance' from kahen `to be far' and tiun ( tik-un ) `age, period of time' from tik `to be old'. The nouns ririnun `length', derived from ririn `to be tall', and temunun `size', derived from temun `to be big', are used in ( exe:modnmlz ).

exe

kowarma=teba temun-un ririn-un ma se me\\
fold= big- nmlz tall- nmlz 3sg dist \\
`Just fold, the size and the length are good.' [conv17_36:41]

exe

Three stative verbs possibly contain a fossilised possessive suffix: kinkinun `small', (ci)caun `small' and temun `big'. These still need to be inflected with -un to be used as nouns, as is illustrated for temun in ( exe:modnmlz ).

Transitive verbs may also be nominalised with -un. This is especially frequent with loan verbs from Malay, as illustrated in ( exe:malayloans ).

exe

xlist
maun `will' (<Indonesian mau `to want')
mencariun `way to make a living' (<Indonesian cari hidup `to make a living', <Malay and Kalamang mencari `to make a living')
mangartiun `understanding' (<Malay and Kalamang mangarti `to understand')
karajangun `job; work' (<Malay and Kalamang karajang `to work')
xlist

exe

To this list can be added the lexical negative construction sukaun ge or sukaun Verb= nin `to not like' (§ sec:lexicalneg ), derived from Malay suka `to like'. Nominalisation with Kalamang transitive verbs is infrequent, but possible. Consider konenenun `memory' from konenen `to remember' in ( exe:konenenun ).

exe
supaya ma neba-un met se mamun=et... konenen-un leng-un\\
so_that 3sg ph-3poss dist.obj leave= remember- nmlz village- 3poss \\
`So that she leaves her whatsit behind, the memories of her village.' [conv8_4:45]

exe

Another infrequent nominalisation occurs with comitative =bon. It occurs on pairs of verbs, for which an overt link is created with comitative =bon, a postposition on the NP. To make the construction, therefore, the verb must be nominalised. In the English translation the verbs remain verbs, and in the Kalamang examples they also seem to have the position and function of verbs. -un is therefore perhaps only a way to make =bon compatible with verbs, without actually changing the function of the verbs.

exe
mu mat metko=a se dan-un=bon kuru masarat-un=bon\\
3pl 3sg.obj dist.loc = foc bury- nmlz=com bring move_landwards- nmlz=com \\
`Did they bury him there? Did they bring him here?' [conv7_2:01]
ka rat-un=bon ka miat-un=bon bisa\\
2sg move- nmlz=com 2sg come- nmlz=com can\\
[When sending a child to buy something] ``Can you go and come back immediately?'' [elic]
exe
summary: A verb can be nominalised with the suffix **-un**, which lets it function as the head of an NP, and this occurs in four main contexts: with **eranun** ‘cannot’, with **stative verbs** to form attributive nouns, with **transitive verbs** especially in Malay loans, and in certain verb pairs linked by the comitative **=bon**. The passage gives examples showing that some nominalisations are required by syntax, while others create nouns such as terms for ‘length,’ ‘size,’ or ‘memory,’ and it notes that in the comitative construction -un may simply make the verb compatible with =bon rather than fully changing its category.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun derivation!agentive

The suffix -et is added to nouns to create agent-denoting nouns, typically describing occupation, residency or origin. It is gender gender neutral. Though productive, at least on place names names!place names, it is not very common. Some examples are given in ( exe:kolet ). Alternatively, origin can be described by adding sontum `person', -ca `man' or -pas `woman' to a noun, as described in § sec:rhcomp.

exe

xlist
canam `man' \\ canam-et `from the man's side of the family'
leng `village' \\ leng-et `villager'
Tamisen `Antalisa (village)' \\ Tamisen-et `Antalisa person'
kol- `outside' \\ kol-et `outsider; stranger'
xlist

exe

There is one corpus example where an agentive noun is derived from a verb, given in ( exe:kamangett ). Several data points suggest a link between agentive nominaliser -et and a more general ``animator''. Many animal names, especially those for insects, end in -et or -let (given in exe:letet ). This is not a productive suffix on animal names, and there is no proof of a diachronic relation with the agentive nominaliser -et. However, note also the animate classifier et- (§ sec:clf ). A speculative relation could be made between donenet `black ant' and -nenen `body hair' (`that which is hairy'), and between kalabet `earth worm' and kalawen `soft' (`that which is soft'). Kedederet `k.o. bird' could be derived from an onomatopoeion onomatopoeion.

exe

xlist
donenet `black ant'
kalabet `earth worm'
kalkalet `mosquito'
kapapet `glassy sweeper (k.o. fish)'
kedederet `k.o. small black bird'
pabalet `fly'
pueselet `spider'
xlist

exe

exe
kamang `to receive treatment from a medicine man' \\ kamang-et `medicine man'

exe
summary: The suffix **-et** forms gender-neutral agentive nouns, typically meaning occupation, residence, or origin; it is productive but not very common, especially with place names. The passage also notes some possible but unproven connections between **-et** and animate or animal-naming patterns, including a single verb-derived example **kamang-et** ‘medicine man.’

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
compound|( noun derivation!compounding binominal|seecompound

A common way to derive nouns is by compounding. Compounds are bases derived from two roots, as introduced in § sec:compounding. All Kalamang compounds are endocentric, which means that the category of the whole is identical to that of one of the constituents. Left-headed compounds, where the first constituent is the head, and right-headed headedness compounds, where the second constituent is the head, both occur, illustrated in ( exe:threecomps ). They are described in § sec:lhcomp and § sec:rhcomp.

exe

xlist
wienar saruam \\
parrotfish?\\
`longnose parrotfish' ( Hipposcarus harid ) left-headed
sayang ror-un \\
nutmeg tree- 3poss \\
`nutmeg tree' right-headed

xlist

exe

Irrespective of type, both constituents need not have an independent meaning. In wienar saruam, wienar is the general word for `parrotfish' (compare wienar tebolkin `roundhead parrotfish', lit. `parrotfish belonging to the reef edge'), but saruam has no translational equivalent.

Noun incorporation is described in § sec:incorp.
summary:
A common way to derive nouns in Kalamang is through compounding, where compounds are formed from two roots. All Kalamang compounds are endocentric, meaning the whole compound has the same category as one of its constituents, and both left-headed and right-headed compounds occur.

The passage also notes that both constituents of a compound do not need to have independent meanings; for example, in *wienar saruam* one element lacks a direct translation. Noun incorporation is treated separately.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
headedness

In left-headed compounds the first constituent is the head. They are subtype compounds, male/female compounds or big/small compounds.

Subtype compounds are those that specify the kind of entity the head noun is. They typically denote plants and animals, as seen in ( exe:subtype ).

exe
subtype compounds
xlist
im selen\\
banana?\\
`kind of banana'
kibi karek\\
sea_cucumber rope\\
`kind of sea cucumber'
wat sasul\\
coconut spoon\\
`young coconut [that one can eat with a spoon]'
pak talawak\\
moon east\\
`new moon'
xlist

exe

Other left-headed compounds are made with the nouns pas `woman', canam `man', emun `mother' and tumun `child'. The first two, exemplified in ( exe:mfcomp ), specify the gender gender of the head noun, and the second two specify relative size, with emun for big things and tumun for small things. This is always relative to another referent, i.e., having a contrastive function. For example, one may talk about one's kewe tumun `house child', which is a small building on the same ground as one's house. `Mother' and `child' are also often used for pairs, such as the two islands south of the biggest Karas island in ( exe:lempuangt ). In Malay, they are named after the protagonists of a tale about a dog ( anjing ) and a cassowary ( kasuari ) who run into the sea and turn into rocks (narr20 in the corpus). The islands are relatively close to each other, and because of the tale are conceived of as a pair.

exe
male/female compounds
xlist
tumun pas-un se gonggung\\
child woman- 3poss call\\
`His daughter called.' [narr21_2:04]
polkayak canam=at dorma\\
papaya man= obj pull_out\\
`Pull out a male papaya tree.' [conv20_31:16]
xlist

big/small compounds
xlist
lempuang-tumun\\
island-child\\
`Pulau Anjing/Dog Island'
lempuang-emun\\
island-mother. 3poss \\
`Pulau Kasuari/Cassowary Island'

xlist
exe
summary: The passage describes left-headed compounds, in which the first constituent is the head. It distinguishes subtype compounds, which identify the kind of entity named by the head noun and often refer to plants or animals, from compounds formed with *pas* ‘woman’, *canam* ‘man’, *emun* ‘mother’, and *tumun* ‘child’, which mark gender or relative size. The size terms are used contrastively and can also express paired entities, such as two related islands.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
headedness

Right-headed compounds include all part-whole compounds, all compounds with a people's name and mang `language', sontum `person' or -ca/-pas `man/woman', and some body parts.

The second constituent of many right-headed compounds is marked by third-person possessive -un. The general associative marker =kin is used to make similar constructions to these. See § sec:asspl.

exe

xlist
kewe mul-un\\
house side- 3poss \\
`the side of the house'
takurera ol-un\\
starfruit leaf- 3poss \\
`starfruit leaf'
xlist
exe

Part-whole compounds are compounds where the second constituent is either a bound root which typically specifies a plant part (§ sec:inal ) or a free root (a word) specifying another part-whole relationship. The second constituent is the head and is marked with third-person possessive marker -un. There is no recorded meaning for bel in am belun `nipple' (given in exe:ambel ), but there is a stative verb belbel `(of a tip) to be sharp'.

exe
part-whole compounds
xlist
sayang tang-un\\
nutmeg seed- 3poss \\
`nutmeg seed'
am bel-un\\
breast tip?- 3poss \\
`nipple'

anggas ror-un\\
door wood- 3poss \\
`doorpost'
xlist
exe

( exe:urkiet ) is a common way to form the meaning `cloud' in Maritime Melanesian Melanesian languages languages schapper2017c.

exe
ur kiet-un\\
wind faeces- 3poss \\
`cloud'

exe

All place names names!place names, such as Kalamang (the biggest Karas island), Lenggon (smaller Karas Islands), Rarait (Seram) and Walaka (Gorom), can be compounded with mang `language', sontum `person' or -ca/-pas `man/woman'. Note that in these right-headed compounds, one cannot use the independent nouns canam `man' and pas `woman'. Another way to derive the name of a people from a place name is with the suffix -et, see § sec:nounorig.

exe
compounds for peoples and languages
xlist
Kalamang-mang\\
Kalamang-language\\
`Kalamang language'
Kalamang-sontum\\
Kalamang-person\\
`Kalamang person'
Kalamang-ca\\
Kalamang-man\\
`Kalamang man'
Kalamang-pas\\
Kalamang-woman\\
`Kalamang woman'
xlist
exe

While most body parts are expressed as part-whole compounds, with the help of -un 3poss, some can be compounded without overt morphology, as illustrated in ( exe:nakedcomp ). It is also grammatical to add -un ` 3poss ' to the second constituent.

exe
body part compounds
xlist
kaden kies\\
body wrap?\\
`vein'
tan laus\\
hand wide\\
`hand palm'
kor kasir\\
leg joint\\
`ankle'
kor-pak\\
leg-moon\\
`knee'
xlist

exe

For many right-headed compounds, the choice between using or not using -un ` 3poss ' is free. They are both compounds because the first constituent cannot be independently marked or inflected.

exe
compounds with and without -un 3poss
xlist
kokok-nar\\
chicken-egg\\
`chicken egg'
kokok nar-un\\
chicken egg\\
`chicken egg'
xlist
exe
compound|)
summary: The passage explains that right-headed compounds in Kalamang include part-whole compounds, compounds naming peoples and languages from place names, and some body-part terms. In many of these compounds, the second element is marked with third-person possessive **-un**, though some can appear without overt morphology or with the associative marker **=kin**; the first element cannot be separately inflected.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
reduplication!nouns|(

Reduplication of nouns is used to create plural plural!nominal nouns (§ sec:plnoun ), to indicate distributivity (§ sec:distrnoun ), to indicate extremity (§ sec:extrnoun ) or to create other nouns by association or nouns expressing in-between states (§ sec:nountonounder ). The derivation of verbs from nouns by means of reduplication is described in § sec:verbder. The formal aspects of reduplication are described in § sec:redup. reduplication!nouns
summary: Noun reduplication is used to form plural nouns, mark distributivity, indicate extremity, and derive other nouns by association or to express in-between states. The text also notes that verb derivation from nouns by reduplication is treated elsewhere, and that the formal properties of reduplication are described in a separate section.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
plural!nominal noun derivation!plural

Though plurality of nominal referents is not obligatorily expressed on nouns, some nouns may be reduplicated to that effect. Most nouns cannot be reduplicated to form a plural, and those that can need not be reduplicated to have a plural referent. plural!nominal

exe

xlist
pes `peel; skin' → pespes `peels; skins; leftovers after peeling'
lempuang `island' → lempuangpuang `islands'
tumun `child' → tumtum `children'
xlist

exe
summary: Plurality is not normally marked obligatorily on nouns, but some nouns can be reduplicated to indicate plurality. However, this is a limited process: most nouns cannot form plurals by reduplication, and even those that can do not have to be reduplicated to refer to more than one entity. Examples include *pes* “peel; skin” → *pespes* “peels; skins,” *lempuang* “island” → *lempuangpuang* “islands,” and *tumun* “child” → *tumtum* “children.”

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun derivation!distributive distributive

Reduplication of nouns that refer to a location can be used to indicate distributivity. ( exe:oskitkit ) and ( exe:osewep ) are from recordings about where certain plants can be found. ( exe:oskitkit ) has a reduplicated oskeit `beach' (from os `sand' and keit `top'), as well as a reduplicated verb kos `to grow' to indicate distribution or habituality (§ sec:verbred ). ( exe:osewep ) has a reduplicated osep `beach' (perhaps from os `sand' and ep `back').

exe
biasa oskeit∼keit=ko kos∼kos=te\\
normally beach∼ distr = loc grow∼ distr = \\
`Normally it grows at the beach.' [narr33_5:42]

ma osep∼ep=ko Tat me reidak\\
3sg beach∼ distr=loc Tat much\\
`It's at the beach. At Tat there are many.' [conv20_48:05]

exe

( exe:rumrum ) makes use of reduplicated tim `edge; tip' (modifying a plant name) to indicate a path.

exe
inier yecie... rumrum-tim∼tim mera se pareir\\
1du.ex return kind_of_plant-edge∼ distr then follow\\
`We returned following the edge of the rumrum plants.' [conv11_2:36]

exe
summary: Reduplication of nouns referring to locations can mark distributivity, as in forms meaning “at the beach,” where the location noun is reduplicated to indicate that something is spread out or occurs in several places. The passage also notes a case where reduplicated *tim* “edge; tip” modifies a plant name to express a path, as in “following the edge of the rumrum plants.”

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun derivation!extremity

Reduplication with the enclitic =tun `very' can be used with nouns referring to a location location to indicate extremity. This is uncommon, and is only found in two instances. With siun `edge', the noun is reduplicated, and with ep `back' the enclitic is reduplicated.

exe

xlist
siun `edge' → siunsiuntun `the very edge'
ep `back' → epduntun `the very back'
xlist

exe
summary: Reduplication with the enclitic =tun ‘very’ can express extremity with nouns referring to locations, but this is uncommon and attested only twice. In one case the noun itself is reduplicated, as in *siun* ‘edge’ → *siunsiuntun* ‘the very edge’, and in the other the enclitic is reduplicated, as in *ep* ‘back’ → *epduntun* ‘the very back’.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun derivation!noun-to-noun

Associative noun-to-noun derivation or noun-to-noun derivation expressing in-between states is rather uncommon. ( exe:donsaun ) illustrates associative derivation.

exe

xlist
don `thing' → dodon `clothes'
saun `night' → sausaun `darkness'
xlist

exe

There are two examples of noun-to-noun derivation which possibly express in-between states. Both are derived from a word for sea (water). Pasirwasir `brackish water' is derived from pasier `sea water', and indicates the state of water in between fresh and salt. The derivation of rangrang `lukewarm' from rang `open sea' is less obvious, but may involve reference to the state of water in between cold (like sea water) and boiling.

exe

xlist
pasier `sea water' → pasirwasir `brackish water'
rang `open sea' → rangrang `lukewarm'
xlist
exe

reduplication!nouns|) noun derivation|) noun|)
summary: Associative noun-to-noun derivation, including derivation that expresses intermediate states, is rare. The passage gives examples such as *don* “thing” → *dodon* “clothes” and *saun* “night” → *sausaun* “darkness,” and notes two possible cases from words for sea: *pasier* “sea water” → *pasirwasir* “brackish water” and *rang* “open sea” → *rangrang* “lukewarm.”

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
noun phrase|(

This section considers the behaviour of the different constituents of the NP. Quantifiers, possessive pronouns, attributive predicates and demonstratives follow the head noun. Nominal possessors precede the head noun. Their mutual order is illustrated in ( exe:npstr ). The place of attributive attribute predicates is tentative due to a shortage of unambiguous instances in the data.

exe
noun-phrase structure\\
( nom.poss ) head (- poss.pron ) ( quant ) ( poss.pron ) ( attr ) ( dem )

exe

Fully saturated NPs such as the one formulated in ( exe:npstr ) are exceedingly uncommon in the data. There is exactly one natural spoken corpus example with three post-nominal modifiers in the NP, illustrated in ( exe:dongdong ).

exe

hukat kon anggon yuwa me paruo dong∼dong-kaning\\
net one 1sg.poss prox make tense∼ ints -very\\
`This one net of mine, make it tight.' [conv5_2:39]

exe

Relative clauses, which are made with the attributive marker =ten, are very rare. They follow the NP head.

In the following sections, I describe the function and syntax of NP modifiers.
summary: The passage describes noun phrase structure, noting that nominal possessors precede the head noun, while quantifiers, possessive pronouns, attributive predicates, and demonstratives follow it. It also says that fully saturated noun phrases are very rare in the data, and that relative clauses marked with =ten are also rare and occur after the noun phrase head.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
possession!nominal
Nominal possessors (§ sec:possphr ) precede the possessed noun. ( exe:unyua ) shows a nominal possessor preceding the head noun ming `oil'.

exe
ka nene ming-un yuwa =at kuet=et\\
2sg grandmother oil- 3poss prox=obj bring= \\
`You bring this oil of granny's.' [conv12_2:21]

exe
summary: In this language, nominal possessors come before the possessed noun. The example shows the possessor “grandmother” preceding the head noun “oil,” meaning “this oil of granny’s.”

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
numeral quantifier|(

Quantifiers (introduced in § sec:wcquantnum ) indicate the quantity of the referent of a NP. They include numeral and non-numeral quantifiers. Quantifiers take the second slot after the noun in the NP, following the possessive suffix. Quantifiers modifying the subject are unmarked, as shown by karuok `three' in ( exe:ladank ) and ikon `few; some' in ( exe:emikon ). Quantifiers may carry a classifier prefix, depending on the noun. ( exe:kanase ) shows the classifier ep- for groups of living beings, on the numeral kon `one', modifying kanas `kind of fish'. For more on classifiers, see § sec:clf.

exe
opa som karuok me mambaran kon ladan kerkap\\
earlier person three stand one shirt red\\
`Earlier, there were three people standing, one [had] a red shirt.' [stim43_17:50]

emumur ikon toni ah ma se me\\
woman. pl some say int 3sg dist \\
`Some of the women say: ``Ah, that's it.''' [narr2_9:51]

kanas ep-kon =a marua ime\\
kind_of_fish clf_group -one= foc move_seawards dist \\
`A school of kanas moves towards that [part of] the sea!' [conv5_0:29]

exe

Quantifiers modifying the object carry a special object marker, -i quantifier object, while the object is marked with the object postposition =at (see § sec:at ). In these cases, the quantifiers appear to be outside the PP, as tentatively indicated in ( exe:kanye ) and ( exe:mingtunat ). postpositional phrase

exe
in marua pas kanyot=at kansuor-i koluk\\
1pl.excl move_seawards exactly giant_clam= obj four- objqnt find\\
`We went to sea and found four giant clams right there.' [narr44_12:37]

mingtun=at bolon-i ko=yuon\\
coconut_oil= obj little- objqnt appl =rub\\
`[You] rub a little coconut oil on.' [narr31_1:32]

exe

In NPs which contain a quantifier and another modifier occupying a later slot, however, the quantifier does not carry -i objqnt. In ( exe:nairmet ), the demonstrative (which is the last possible element of the NP) carries object marking, and the quantifiers again appear to be inside the NP.

exe
mu yap_seran-un nak- eir met toni pasor=ta eba mu nan=et\\
3pl yam- 3poss clf_fruit1 -two dist.obj want fry= then 3pl consume= \\
`They want to fry those two yams and then they want to eat.' [conv10_16:02]

exe

The quantifier object -i should not be analysed as the predicate linker =i (§ sec:mvci ), because it only occurs on quantifiers modifying object NPs or acting as NP heads, and never on subjects or any peripheral arguments. The exact relation of quantifiers to the NP and the predicate is an area for further research. Japanese and Korean have similar phenomena, where quantifiers can be both inside and outside the NP kang2002.

The head noun can be elided when the nominal referent can be retrieved from the context, so that the numeral numeral becomes the head of the NP. This is shown in ( exe:ladank ) above for kon `one' and eir `two' in ( exe:eirnau ), where the two animals have been extensively referred to earlier in the conversation, and are visible in pictures in front of the speakers. In ( exe:mekua ), the numeral head is modified by a demonstrative.

exe

eir nau=namanghadap\\
two recp =face\\
`Two [animals] face each other.' [stim14_2:09]

kon wa me kuat=nin\\
one prox strong= neg \\
`This one isn't strong.' [conv2_7:06]

exe

The quantifier object marker also remains in place if the object is elided, as in ( exe:nuru ).

exe
wowa Nuru mu Subj taukon-i Obj an Pred \\
aunt Nura 3pl some- objqnt 1sg \\
`Aunt Nuru's family gave me some' [conv12_8:39]

exe

In a few cases, numeral quantifiers form a compound compound with the noun. ( exe:yuolreitkon ) has the compound yuol reitkon `the hundredth day', which is an important day in the commemoration of deceased people. The fact that it is a compound is evidenced by the object marker on the numeral.

exe

tok yuol reitkon =at=a nawanggar\\
still day hundred= obj=foc wait\\
`[We are] still waiting for the hundredth day.' [narr1_4:53]

exe

Quantifiers are discussed in more detail in Chapter ch:quant. quantifier|)
summary:
Quantifiers, including numeral and non-numeral forms, express the quantity of an NP’s referent and normally occupy the second position in the NP after the possessive suffix. Quantifiers modifying subjects are unmarked, but object quantifiers take a special marker -i, which appears only with object NPs or NP heads and not with subjects or peripheral arguments; quantifiers can also take classifier prefixes depending on the noun.

The passage further notes that a noun may be omitted when recoverable from context, allowing the numeral itself to function as the NP head, and that the object marker can still remain even if the object is elided. In a few cases, numeral quantifiers form compounds with nouns, as shown by object marking on the numeral.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
possession!pronominal

Besides nominal possessors, there are two adnominal markers of possession: nominal possessive suffixes and freestanding possessive pronouns. They are described in detail in Chapter ch:poss. Possessive suffixes attach to the head noun, as in ( exe:keweant ).

exe

an kewe-an temun =at paruo\\
1sg house- 1sg.poss big= obj make\\
`I am making my big house.' [elic_adj_29]

exe

Possessive pronouns occupy a slot between head nouns and demonstratives (more precisely, between quantifiers and attributively used verbs, but no example illustrating this is available). ( exe:gamka ) illustrates a possessive pronoun preceding a demonstrative.

exe

gambar kain yuwane \\
picture 2sg.poss prox \\
`this picture of yours' [stim43_0:26]

exe
summary: The passage says that, in addition to nominal possessors, there are two adnominal possession markers: possessive suffixes and freestanding possessive pronouns. Possessive suffixes attach to the head noun, while possessive pronouns occur between the head noun and demonstratives, as shown by the example meaning “this picture of yours.”

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
demonstrative|(

As introduced in § sec:wcdem, Kalamang has five demonstrative roots: proximal wa, distal me, far distal owa, and the elevationals yawe ` down ' and osa ` up '. These can all be modified with locative =ko and lative =ka (Chapter ch:dems ). Most, but not all forms can be preceded by yu- and followed by -ne without a change in meaning. The anaphoric demonstrative opa functions to mark referents that represent shared knowledge or have been previously mentioned. It does not occur with any affixes. A detailed description of demonstratives is found in Chapter ch:dems.

Adnominal demonstratives fill the last slot in the NP. The following examples show the demonstratives in adnominal function. When they modify a noun in object function, the demonstrative roots carry -t, a remnant of object marker =at.

( exe:demadd ) and ( exe:pulorc ) illustrate the proximal and distal forms. In ( exe:demadd ), the speaker points to a woman in a picture in front of him, and uses the proximal form to modify enem `woman'. In ( exe:pulorc ), pulor-ca `your betel', which is not currently visible, is modified with the distal demonstrative me. In ( exe:donowa ), the far distal owa is used to modify don `thing', which refers to a herb which one can collect at a neighbouring beach.

ma enem wat =a tu\\
3sg woman prox.obj=foc hit\\
`He hits this woman.' [stim6_11:45]

an pulor-ca met parua=ta\\
1sg betel_vine- 2sg.poss dist.obj pluck= \\
`I plucked that betel vine of yours.' [conv12_8:15]

don owa =ba mambon\\
thing fdist = foc exist \\
`That thing over there is there.' [narr3_3:18]

Elevationals are commonly used in their locative form to modify nouns.

exe
kewe-un yawetko ma tua=ta me\\
house- 3poss down.loc 3sg live= \\
`He lives in his house down there.' [narr24_0:21]
ma sara bo karop-un osatko \\
3sg ascend go branch- 3poss up.loc \\
`He climbs to the branch up there.' [conv12_16:39]
exe

The demonstrative opa modifies goras `crow' in ( exe:gorasopa ), indicating that the crow being referred to is the same one that was mentioned earlier in the story.

exe
goras opa melelu ror-kitko kome bara∼bara\\
crow ana sit tree-top. loc look down∼ prog \\
`That crow sits in the tree looking down.' [narr39_2:20]

exe
NPs with demonstratives almost never contain other nominal modifiers; ( exe:dongdong ) above is one of the few in the corpus. demonstrative|)
summary:
Kalamang has five demonstrative roots: proximal wa, distal me, far distal owa, and the elevationals yawe ‘down’ and osa ‘up’. These can take locative =ko and lative =ka, and most can also be bracketed by yu- and -ne without changing meaning; the anaphoric demonstrative opa is different in that it marks previously mentioned or shared referents and does not take affixes.

Adnominal demonstratives occur in the final slot of the noun phrase, and when they modify an object noun they take -t as a remnant of the object marker. Elevational demonstratives are commonly used in locative form, and NPs with demonstratives almost never include other nominal modifiers.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
attribute!predicative

All verbal predicates can be used attributively (§ sec:wcverb ). Attributive clitic =ten is attached to predicates when they are used attributively both in subject position, as in ( exe:attradj a), and in object position, as in ( exe:attradj b). See also § sec:wcverb.

exe

xlist

sontum ririn= ten me sor=at na\\
person tall= at dist fish= obj eat\\
`That tall person eats fish.' [elic]

an som ririn= ten met komet=kin\\
1sg person tall= at dist.obj see= \\
`I want to see that tall person.' [elic]

xlist
exe

Often, predicates modifying a noun carry the attributive marker =ten. Examples include the locative leng=ko `in the village' in ( exe:lengkoren ), reduplicated towari `young' in ( exe:towawa ) and lu `cold' in ( exe:luren ). However, common attributes like colours, (ci)caun/kinkinun `small' and temun `big' may modify a noun without the use of =ten, exemplified for kinkinun `small' in ( exe:rorkin ) (see also § sec:wcverb ).

exe
mungkin proyek kegiatan leng=ko=ten \\
maybe project activity village= loc = at \\
`Or maybe a project with an activity that is in the village.' [narr45_2:27]

pebis towari∼wa=ten mara\\
woman young∼ red = at move_landwards\\
`The young women came to the shore.' [narr19_3:01]

se pasa lu=ten=at nan=i koyet\\
rice cold= at=obj consume= finish\\
`After eating cold rice...' [conv10_3:40]

ror kinkinun saerak\\
wood small neg_exist \\
`There is no small wood.' [conv12_1:10]

exe

It is quite uncommon for a predicate to be used attributively; Kalamang speakers prefer to express monovalent stative non-agentive characteristics predicatively. It is therefore not surprising that there are no spontaneous utterances with more than one attributive predicate modifying a noun. In elicited material, attributive predicates are not overtly conjoined.

exe
kip temun kuskap sasuak kiem\\
snake big black slippery flee\\
`The big black slippery snake fled.' [elic_adj_37]

exe

The position of attributively used predicates in the NP appears to be between possessive pronouns and demonstratives. There are corpus examples that show an attributive predicate after a noun modifying a noun as in ( exe:yarpos ), after a quantifier as in ( exe:ar1 ) and after a possessive marker as in ( exe:esatem ), as well as before a demonstrative as in ( exe:tuaren0 ) and ( exe:pepun ).

exe
mu in=at pareir bo yar-pos nerunggo yar-pos temun o\\
3pl 1pl.excl=obj follow go rock-hole inside. loc rock-hole big emph \\
`They followed us inside the hole, a big hole.' [narr40_7:13]

inier bo ror opa temun ror ar-kon temun \\
2du.ex go tree ana big tree clf_stem -one big\\
`We went [to] the big tree, the big tree.' [narr40_3:27]

esa anggon temun=a an=at gonggung\\
father 1sg.poss big= foc 1sg=obj call\\
`My father's older brother calls me.' [conv10_9:20]

sontum tua=ten opa me Ayah Panggil esun ma mat terima\\
person old= at Ayah Panggil father. 3poss 3sg 3sg.obj welcome\\
`That old person, Ayah Panggil's father welcomes her.' [conv8_3:57]

mu pep-un karuar=ten met nan=i koyet\\
3sg pig- 3poss smoke_dry= at dist.obj consume= finish\\
`He ate their smoked pig.' [narr28_1:54]

exe

This would place the attributive predicate in the slot between the possessive pronoun and the demonstrative. In elicited clauses, however, the attributive predicate was often placed right after the noun, often preceding the quantifier. The following is the result of some elicited clauses with two, three or four modifiers:

exe

xlist
N ATR DEM Q
N POSS ATR DEM Q
N Q DEM
N ATR Q DEM
N ATR Q DEM
N Q ATR DEM
N ATR Q [elic_dem]
xlist
exe

A definitive analysis of the position of attributively used predicates in the NP awaits more data.
summary:
Attributive clitic =ten can attach to verbal predicates when they modify a noun, whether the modified noun is in subject or object position. Although many predicates can be used attributively, this is relatively uncommon, and speakers usually prefer predicative expression for stative, non-agentive properties; common modifiers like colours, “small,” and “big” may sometimes appear without =ten.  

The text also notes that the placement of attributive predicates within the noun phrase is not fully settled: corpus data suggest a position between possessive pronouns and demonstratives, but elicited examples often place the attributive predicate immediately after the noun, sometimes before quantifiers. A final analysis of this position is left open pending more data.

chapter: Nouns, noun phrases and postpositional phrases
text:
relative clause

A relative clause is a NP modifier in which one of the arguments corefers the head noun. Kalamang does not have a dedicated relative clause marker, but relative clauses may be marked with the attributive marker =ten (§ sec:attr ). Most attributive examples in § sec:attr, which are with intransitive verbs, may be paraphrased as a relative clause.

What is expressed by relativised clauses in some languages is typically done with biclausal constructions or non-final constructions in Kalamang. This is reflected in elicitation. In ( exe:jenden ), the speaker was asked for a translation of `this thing I bought was bad' (Malay barang ini yang saya beli tidak bagus ), and gave a biclausal construction linked by conjunction ba `but'. ( exe:komeraa ) is the translation given for `the children that I saw went to sea' (Malay anak yang saya lihat pi di laut ), and is a biclausal construction involving the verb kome `to see' marked with non-final =ta.

exe
don wa=at=a an jien ba ten\\
thing prox=obj=foc 1sg buy but bad\\
`This thing, I bought [it] but [it] is bad.' [elic_rel_10]

tumun opa me an kome= ta, mu wilak=ka marua\\
child 1sg see= 3pl sea= lat move_seawards\\
`Having seen those children, they went to sea.' [elic_rel_49]

exe

There are a few indications, however, that relativisation of clauses headed by transitive verbs is possible. There is one natural spoken corpus example that seems to display a relativisation of the object of a transitive clause.

exe
som=a tama=ba tamat-un=at nasibur= ten ma tok tamat=at koi naputus\\
person= foc q = foc recital_end- 3poss=obj recite= at 3sg first recital_end= obj then cut\\
`Whoever is reciting the end of their recital, he cuts off the end of the recital.' [narr1_4:05]
exe

In elicitation with pictures of two or three people performing different actions, one of which had an object (e.g. a flower) on their head, speakers sometimes opted to answer the question `where is the [object]?' with a relative clause. Only subjects occur as the antecedent of the relativised clause. Note that the dependent marked with =ten precedes the head, whereas in attributive constructions (discussed in § sec:attr ) it follows the head.

exe
bunga pas gol=at sempang= ten nakal keirunggo\\
flower woman ball= obj kick= at head on_top_of\\
`The flower is on the head of the woman who kicks the ball.' [elic_foc_3]

kawir canam im=at nan= ten nakal keirunggo\\
hat man banana= obj consume= at head on_top_of\\
`The hat is on the head of the man who eats the banana.' [elic_foc_5]
exe

However, biclausal alternatives are also frequently found in such a task, as in the following two examples.

exe
bunga wa me pas nakal kerunggo pas opa me botal=at sempang\\
flower prox woman head on_top_of woman bottle= obj kick\\
`This flower is on the woman's head. That woman kicks a bottle.' [elic_foc_2]
kuda eir kon me bunga nakal keirunggo kon me ge\\
horse two one flower head on_top_of one not\\
`There are two horses. One has a flower on its head. One doesn't.' [elic_foc_8]
exe
summary: Kalamang has no dedicated relative clause marker; relative clauses may instead be marked with the attributive marker =ten, and many attributive constructions with intransitive verbs can be paraphrased as relative clauses. In practice, however, meanings that are expressed by relative clauses in other languages are often rendered in Kalamang with biclausal or non-final constructions, though some evidence suggests that relativisation of transitive clauses is possible. The data indicate that only subjects occur as antecedents of relativised clauses, and that =ten-marked dependents precede the head noun, unlike attributive constructions where they follow it.
