summary: Imperatives are directive speech acts used for orders and commands, and they are marked by the enclitic =te on the predicate. An imperative clause may include an explicit subject (the addressee) or omit it, and imperative forms are also used for hortatives, not just orders. Movement verbs ending in -a have special imperative forms in -ei, and give-constructions form the imperative by adding =te to the recipient, with benefactive marking appearing before it if present.

text:
negation|(

This section describes clausal negation. It starts with a description of standard negation with negator =nin, the negation of declarative verbal main clauses miestamo2005, in § sec:standneg. It then goes on to describe negation in non-declarative and non-verbal clauses, in § sec:negnondecl and § sec:negnonv. Dedicated negative verbs with the meanings `not know', `not like' and `cannot' are described in § sec:lexicalneg. Two negative polarity items are treated in § sec:negpol. This account of Kalamang negative clauses is an adaptation of a part of.
summary: This section presents clausal negation in Kalamang, beginning with standard negation using the negator =nin in declarative verbal main clauses. It then outlines negation in non-declarative and non-verbal clauses, as well as lexical negative verbs meaning “not know,” “not like,” and “cannot,” and two negative polarity items.

subsection: Negation of declarative verbal main clauses
text:
Negation of declarative verbal main clauses (also known as standard negation, ) is achieved by adding the negator =nin to the predicate. Example ( exe:sem ) contrasts an affirmative and a negated clause with the stative verb sem `to be afraid'.

ma sem\\
3sg be_afraid\\
`She's afraid.' [conv11_2:14]

ma sem= nin \\
3sg be_afraid= neg \\
`She's not afraid.' [narr40_16:33]

Examples ( exe:negv ) and ( exe:negadj ) show a negated transitive verb and a negated intransitive stative verb. In both cases, the constituent order of the non-negated counterpart is the same.

ma yuon=at konat= nin \\
3sg sun= obj see= neg \\
`He didn't see the sun.' [stim7_22:55]

wa me mang= nin \\
prox bitter= neg \\
`This one isn't bitter.' [narr34_3:10]

Give-constructions, with a zero morpheme `give', can be negated by adding =nin to the zero morpheme, as in ( exe:kaanin ).

an me ka an ∅= nin o\\
1sg 2sg 1sg give= neg emph \\
`Me, you didn't give me!' [conv12_17:43]

When the recipient is a noun instead of a pronoun, the recipient is followed by the benefactive enclitic =ki. In a negated clause, the zero morpheme follows the benefactive enclitic, and =nin is attached to the zero morpheme, as illustrated in ( exe:kinin ).

guru tok dodon=at di=tumun=ki ∅= nin \\
teacher yet thing= obj caus =child= ben give= neg \\
`The teacher hasn't given the children the gift yet.' [elic_give_15]

On a surface level, it looks as if =nin is cliticised to pronouns and postpositions in give-constructions, but underlyingly negation of give-constructions works exactly the same as other standard verbal negation: by adding =nin to the predicate.

Negative clauses differ from affirmatives in that they do not allow the same verbal marking. The enclitic =kin (§ sec:kin ), used in affirmative clauses for the expression of volition and imminent situations, is incompatible with negator =nin. This is illustrated in example ( exe:kinneg ). The range of semantic distinctions that =kin can express is lost, or underspecified, once a clause is negated (`neutralisation' in ).. Thus, ( exe:turnin ) is ambiguous between a reading that the child does not want to eat or is not about to eat, and a plain negation of the verb `to eat', i.e. `the child does not eat'. Note that for explicitly expressing `not want', the Kalamang speaker can use a dedicated expression suka - poss ge, as described in § sec:lexicalneg.

[*]
tumun muap= kin=nin \\
child eat= =neg \\
`The child doesn't want to eat.'

[]
tumun muap= nin \\
child eat= neg \\
`The child doesn't (want to) eat.' [elic_neg_1]

Irrealis mood, indicated by enclitic =et on the predicate, is compatible with negator =nin. It always gets the reading of a negative conditional conditional, whereas irrealis mood in affirmative clauses is not exclusively used for conditionals (§ sec:et, sec:condclause ).

exe
ki tok newer= nin=et ki sabua nerungga rat-un eranun\\
2sg yet pay= neg = 2pl tent inside. lat move- nmlz cannot\\
`If you haven't paid yet, you cannot go inside the tent.' [narr5_2:18]

exe

At least two of the five aspectual markers are compatible with negated verbs, whereby the aspect takes scope over negation. The aspectual word tok `yet; still; first' (a.k.a. nondum nondum, ) can be combined with a negated verb to form the meaning `not yet', and iamitive iamitive se (sometimes translatable as `already') takes the meaning `not any more' in negated clauses. For further illustration of the interaction of these aspectual markers with negation, see § sec:setok. nondum iamitive
summary: Standard negation in declarative verbal main clauses is formed by attaching the negator =nin to the predicate, and this same strategy applies to ordinary verbs and to zero-marked give-constructions. In negated clauses, the affirmative enclitic =kin cannot occur, so its volitional or imminent meanings are neutralized, whereas irrealis =et is compatible with negation and yields a negative conditional interpretation. The aspectual markers tok and se can also combine with negation, with meanings like “not yet” and “not any more,” respectively.

text:
prohibitive

Content questions (§ sec:opq ) are negated with negator =nin, as illustrated in ( exe:kabnin ).

exe
naman=a kewe=at kabarat= nin \\
who= foc house= obj sweep= neg \\
`Who doesn't want to sweep the house?' [elic_neg_20]

exe

polar question Polar questions (§ sec:polq ) are formed by adding ye ge, literally `or not', at the end of an affirmative clause, as in ( exe:yege1 ). Ye ge is neutral in the sense that there is no expectation of either a positive or negative answer. Leaving ye ge out but keeping question intonation intonation is possible, but not often encountered.

mu kat gonggung ter-nan ye ge \\
3pl 2sg.obj call tea-consume or not\\
`Are they calling you for tea?' [conv12_20:16]

To express a negative expectation to an answer (as opposed to confirmation-seeking, § sec:confquest ), one may use negator =nin. Note that there are no occurrences of this type in the natural spoken corpus.

ma pasa=at nat= nin \\
3sg rice= obj consume= neg \\
`Doesn't he eat rice?' [elic_neg_15]

There are no occurrences of negated alternative questions.

Prohibitives, the negative counterpart of imperatives (§ sec:impcla ), have a dedicated construction involving pronominal suffix -mun and clitic =in on the predicate. Note that a combination of -mun and negator =nin is ungrammatical. Example ( exe:proh1 ) illustrates a prohibitive clause. See also § sec:proh.

ka- mun koyal= in \\
2sg-proh disturb= proh \\
`Don't you disturb!' [conv9_10:05]
summary:
The passage describes how negation interacts with different question types and prohibitives. Content questions are negated with the negator =nin, while polar questions are formed with the clause-final particle ye ge ‘or not’; ye ge is neutral, though it can be omitted with only question intonation.  

To express a negative expectation in a polar question, =nin may be used, but this type is not attested in the spoken corpus, and there are no negated alternative questions. Prohibitives have a special construction using the pronominal suffix -mun and the clitic =in on the predicate, and combining -mun with =nin is ungrammatical.

text:
negation!non-verbal clause

Non-verbal clauses may have a NP headed by a noun, a demonstrative demonstrative clause or a quantifier as predicate, or a noun inflected with the locative or similative postposition (§ sec:nomclau to § sec:sim ). Locative and similative predicates can be negated with negator =nin. This also counts for adverbial demonstratives. Predicative NPs may be negated with negator =nin or with clause-final propositional negator ge. Possessive and demonstrative clauses must be negated with propositional negator ge. Quantifiers are not negated. Not-having and negative existential clauses are made with negative existential verb saerak.

( exe:negloc ) is a negated locative, ( exe:mengganin ) a negated lative demonstrative, ( exe:inggonggonin ) a negated animate locative, ( exe:wisenggap ) a negated similative and ( exe:mindinin ) a negated manner adverbial.

ma ewun naun-kit=ko= nin \\
3sg root. 3poss soil-inside= loc = neg \\
`Its root is not inside the soil.' [narr34_4:58]

tete Manggan mu tok mengga= nin weinun\\
grandfather Manggan 3pl yet dist.lat=neg too\\
`[I] haven't yet been to grandfather Manggan's either.' [conv9_24:27]

pengalaman kon yume sampi in=konggo= nin \\
experience one dist until 1pl.excl=an.loc=neg \\
`That experience hasn't reached us yet.' [narr26_15:54]

wise=kap= nin \\
long_time_ago= sim=neg \\
`It's not like it used to be.' [conv9_32:32]

mindi= nin \\
like_that= neg \\
`It's not like that.' [conv7_10:11]

Clauses with a NP as predicate, typically clauses of proper inclusion or ascriptive clauses, may be negated with negator =nin or with propositional negator ge. Consider ( exe:guruneg ). What the (pragmatic) difference between the two constructions is remains for further research.

dun-an me me guru ge \\
cross.sex.sibling- 1sg.poss dist teacher not\\
`That sibling of mine is not a teacher.' [elic_neg_26]

ma me guru= nin \\
3sg teacher= neg \\
`He is not a teacher.' [elic_neg_26]

Possessives and demonstratives in predicate function may not be negated with negator =nin, but must be negated with propositional negator ge. This is illustrated for possessive clauses in ( exe:posneg ).

[*]
don me anggon= nin \\
thing dist 1sg.poss=neg \\
`That stuff isn't mine.' [elic_neg_7]

[]
don me anggon ge \\
thing dist 1sg.poss not\\
`That stuff isn't mine.' [elic_neg_7]

While the proposition `that stuff is mine' is negated in ( exe:anggonge ), non-possession (i.e. not-having) is expressed with negative existential saerak.

tumtum-un saerak \\
children- 1pl.excl.poss neg.exist \\
`We don't have children.' [narr23_6:35]

quantifier Quantifiers are not negated, but some have negative counterparts. The negative counterpart of tebonggan `all' is negative existential saerak. The negative counterpart of reidak `much; many' is reingge `not much; not many'. The latter contains the (prenasalised) morpheme ge `no(t)'.

Finally, existential clauses are negated with negative existential saerak. Examples ( exe:sorsaerak ) and ( exe:saerak ) show existential negation. Saerak is the opposite of existential mambon, as shown in example ( exe:mamsae ). It is ungrammatical to combine either mambon or saerak with negator =nin. Saerak has a slightly more differentiated use than mambon. For non-possession, saerak is obligatory, whereas for affirmative possessive clauses mambon only stresses the presence of a possessed item, but is not necessary to express possession.

sor saerak \\
fish neg_exist \\
`There is no fish.' [conv9_0:55]

karena pak saerak karek=ki=a kanie\\
because nail neg_exist string= ins=foc tie\\
`Because there were no nails [we] tied with string.' [narr7_1:03]

utkon kadok-un mambon utkon muin saerak \\
some cloth- 3poss exist some 3pl.poss neg_exist \\
`Some had their cloths, some didn't have theirs.' [narr40_19:28]

The aspectual particle se `already' and the aspectual word tok `yet; still; first' combine with saerak as illustrated in ( exe:sesaerak ) and ( exe:toksaerak ): they get the meaning `not any more' and `not yet' respectively.

ma nan=et me me tadon se saerak \\
3sg consume= dist cough neg_exist \\
`If they drink that, the cough disappears [is not anymore].' [narr31_2:57]

pitis tok saerak \\
money yet neg_exist \\
`The money isn't there yet.' [narr45_1:06]
summary:
The passage describes how different types of non-verbal clauses are negated. Locative, similative, and some adverbial demonstrative predicates take the negator =nin; predicative NPs may take either =nin or clause-final ge, while possessive and demonstrative clauses require ge, and quantifiers are not negated but may have special negative counterparts.

It also states that non-possession and negative existential clauses are expressed with the negative existential verb saerak, which cannot combine with =nin. Saerak is used for existential negation and with aspectual elements to mean ‘not anymore’ or ‘not yet’.

negation!lexical

Apart from negative existential saerak (the opposite of existential mambon ), described in § sec:negnonv, there are three inherently negative verbal constructions: suka - poss ge `not want; not agree', Verb- nmlz eranun `cannot' and komahal `not know'. These meanings are all common among dedicated negative verbs cross-linguistically veselinova2013pres. They are listed with their positive counterparts below. Negation of any of the verbs described in this section, whether positive or negative forms, with negator =nin is ungrammatical. However, the construction suka - poss neg `to not want; to not agree' may combine with a predicate negated with =nin.

exe

=kin volitional
suka - poss V= neg / ge `to not want; to not agree'

eranun `cannot'

komahal `to not know'

Suka - poss Verb= neg is a dedicated negative construction that means `to not want; to not agree'. The construction is made with the borrowed verb suka (<Indonesian suka `to like', but not in use with that meaning in Kalamang), nominalised by inflection with a possessive suffix and followed by a negated verb. It could be paraphrased as `is not of pron 's liking'. The third-person possessive suffix -un can be used for all subjects. A speaker can, however, choose to inflect suka with another person corresponding with the subject, as in ( exe:parinin ).

sontum haus ba an suka-n-an parin= nin \\
person thirsty but 1sg like- - 1sg.poss sell= neg \\
`People are thirsty [keen to buy] but I don't want to sell.' [narr42_34:03]

When the predicate is lacking, the construction can be made with ge `no', as in ( exe:leka ).

canam opa me mat narorar ba lek suka-un ge \\
man 3sg.obj lead but goat want- 3poss no\\
`That man is leading it, but the goat doesn't want.' [stim31_0:51]

The inflections of suka for all persons are given in Table tab:sukaungge. Note that there is an extra phoneme /n/ between suka and the first-person possessive suffix -an. It is not clear where this /n/ comes from or what it means. It might be epenthetic, inserted to prevent the first-person possessive marker from disappearing (without the /n/, the first-person form would surface as sukangge ). See also § sec:possprob for a discussion of unexplained phonemes on possessed nouns.

As for the lexical opposite of `not want; not agree', there is a verb lo `to consent; to like', but it is rather uncommon. An example is given in ( exe:lo ). Wishes and desires are more commonly expressed with volitional =kin, which is an irrealis marker that is among other functions used as a volitional marker, see example ( exe:natkin ). As we have seen in section sec:standneg, volitional =kin and negator =nin are incompatible.

an bo mu et-un=at paning paning=i koyet mu se lo \\
1sg go 3sg canoe- 3poss=obj ask_for ask_for= finish 3pl consent\\
`I went to ask for their canoe; after asking, they consented.' [narr8_0:12]

bal napikir an sor=at nat= kin \\
dog think 1sg fish= obj consume= \\
`The dog thinks: ``I want to eat the fish.''' [stim1_0:34]

In the pair bisa `can'/ eranun `cannot', we are dealing with a Malay form again, but this time for the positive form: bisa also means `can' in Malay. But whereas bisa in Malay is negated with standard negation marker tidak ( tidak bisa `cannot'), Kalamang has a dedicated form, eranun. The use of eranun triggers nominalisation of the negated proposition with -un ` nmlz '. (This is also the suffix that eranun itself seems to carry, but if that is so, it has lost its meaning.) Eranun is clause-final. Consider examples ( exe:bisa ) and ( exe:ningkabor ). One could also translate the construction Verb- nmlz eranun as `V-ing isn't possible', such that example ( exe:ningkabor ) translates as `toilet-going isn't possible.'

ka marua hukat yume bisa \\
2sg move_seawards fishing_net dist can\\
`Can you go seawards with the fishing net?' [conv1_2:56]

ning-kabor pasiengga bot-un eranun \\
sick-stomach to_beach go- nmlz cannot\\
`[If you have] stomachache [you] cannot go to the toilet.' [conv20_15:58]

This is a clause-initial interjection interjection uttered at high pitch pitch which expresses indignation, and not a verb like komahal.

yeso ka-tain=a gonggin \\
dunno 2sg -alone- foc know\\
`I don't know, only you know.' [conv12_18:43]

mother where int mother 1pl.excl =too not_know\\
`Where's mother?' `Eh, mother, we don't know either.' [narr40_5:19]

summary:
The passage describes three inherently negative verbal constructions in Kalamang: suka-poss Verb=neg or ge ‘not want; not agree,’ eranun ‘cannot,’ and komahal ‘not know.’ It notes that standard negation with =nin is ungrammatical with these verbs, though suka-poss neg can combine with a separately negated predicate.

It explains that suka-poss Verb=neg is built from a borrowed verb suka plus possessive inflection and a negated verb, while eranun is a dedicated clause-final negative form derived from a nominalized proposition. The passage also contrasts these forms with their positive counterparts and notes that wishes and desires are more commonly expressed with the volitional marker =kin than with the rarer verb lo ‘to consent; to like.’

text:
Kalamang has two negative polarity negative polarity items: -barak `any' and don kon∼kon `any'. -barak `any' is a negative polarity item that has to be accompanied by a negated predicate or dedicated negative verb, such as konatnin `not see' in ( exe:lampurbarak ) or jietnin `not get' in ( exe:konbarak ). Som konbarak `no-one' in ( exe:nobody ) could be paraphrased as `not any person'.

lampur- barak ma konat= nin \\
lamp-any 3sg see= neg \\
`He didn't see any lamp.' [stim7_29:22]

sairarar reidak ba kon- barak an jiet= nin \\
lobster many but one-any 1sg get= neg \\
`There were many lobsters but I didn't get any.' [elic_neg]

som kon- barak karajang-un eranun \\

The same suffix is used with the meanings `too' and `even', in which cases it is not a negative polarity item.

Don kon∼kon `any' (lit `thing one∼ red ') can be used with a negative verb or negated predicate (example exe:donkonkon ), or can be negated itself (example exe:dkonkon2 ). (For indefinite pronouns, see § sec:quantinfl.) indefinite pronoun!negation

text:
variation!syntax

Two common patterns of variation apply to Kalamang clausal structure. The first is elision of arguments, and the second is reordering of constituents to mark topics and anti-topics. Arguments that are retrievable from the context may be elided, especially in dialogues. This is described in § sec:syntel. The marking of topic and anti-topic is described in § sec:leftd.
summary: Kalamang clausal structure shows two common kinds of variation: elision of arguments and reordering of constituents to mark topics and anti-topics. Arguments that can be recovered from context may be left out, especially in dialogue, and topic/anti-topic marking is discussed elsewhere in the grammar.

text:
elision

In natural spoken Kalamang, when retrievable from the context, either the subject or the object may be elided, depending on which stays the same across clauses or utterances.

An example of subject elision elision!subject is given in ( exe:subel ). The first clause contains both subject and object. The object and predicate are repeated in the next clause as an instance of tail-head linkage tail-head linkage (§ sec:tailhead ). In the second and third clause, the subject is elided.

exe
Mu he erat dimarua. Erat dimarua, kaiat disara.\\
mu se et=at di=marua et=at di=marua kai=at di=sara\\
3pl canoe= obj caus =move_seawards canoe= obj caus =move_seawards firewood= obj caus =ascend\\
`They moved the canoe towards the water. Moved the canoe towards the water, put the firewood on.' [narr19_1:32]

exe

Subject elision is also possible when the subject has been mentioned by another speaker. Consider the following dialogue, where speaker B responds to speaker A eliding the transitive subject (the first response of speaker B) and the intransitive subject (the second response of speaker B).

exe

xlist
A:
taman-un mat ajak=te kasi minuman\\
friend- 3poss 3sg.obj invite= give drink\\
`His friends invite him, give him drinks.'

B:
mat nacoba\\
3sg.obj try\\
`[ They ] try him'

A:
nacoba to ma toni ma se tobat\\
try tag 3sg say 3sg repent\\
`Try, right, he says he repents.'

B:
tobat yor se koyet\\
repent true finish\\
`[ He ] repents, true, finished.' [stim6_24:05]

In procedural descriptions, the subject may be elided throughout the whole text, being generic or non-referential. Consider the beginning of the monologue of a woman explaining how to weave baskets in ( exe:zeropro ). There is no subject, and throughout the whole explanation she does not introduce one.

exe

kiem=at paruot=kin... gous=at potman\\
basket= obj make=... bamboo= obj cut\\
`Making a basket. [ One ] cuts the bamboo.' [narr11_0:04]

exe

The first-person inclusive clusivity pronoun also occurs in a generic sense. In some stretches of discourse, it occurs once every now and then, being left out for a few clauses in a row, as in ( exe:genericwe ), a description of how traditional houses were built. Here, pi `we' does not refer to a specific group of people building a house on a specific occasion, but is a generic pronoun referring to whoever used to build houses the traditional way.

summary: In natural spoken Kalamang, either the subject or the object may be elided when it is recoverable from context, depending on which participant remains the same across clauses or utterances. The passage illustrates subject elision in linked clauses, dialogues, procedural texts, and generic uses of the inclusive pronoun, and object elision when an already mentioned object continues to be understood in later discourse.

text:
topic
The reordering of arguments is used to mark topics and anti-topics. Topics can be marked by fronting or by doubling the subject NP, and anti-topics are at the right edge of the clause.

A topic topic is ``an entity that the speaker identifies, about which information... is then given''. A topic may be marked by fronting the topicalised constituent. In addition, it may be marked with topic marker me (§ sec:discme ). If the constituent is a subject, or a recipient in a give-construction, it is repeated in the main clause. This kind of fronting is only found with first-person pronoun an. A fronted subject is exemplified in ( exe:anmean ) and a fronted recipient in ( exe:leftd2 ). Fronted objects, in contrast, are not repeated in the main clause. ( exe:kiunatme ) has a fronted object with topic marker me, and ( exe:leftd3 ) has a fronted object without topic marker. Topic marker me is described in § sec:discme.
focus Focused constituents can be marked with focus marker =a or =ba. The constituents remain in their usual position in the clause. Focus is described in § sec:a.

exe

an me an kona watko komana=et kanggir-un=ko to\\
1sg 1sg think prox.loc skewer= eye- 3poss=loc right\\
`As for me, I think you skewer it here, in the eye, right?' [stim15_4:32]

an me ka an ∅=nin o\\
1sg 2sg 1sg give= neg emph \\
`Me, you didn't give me.' [conv12_17:44]

kiun=at me ma gonggung=te ma kirarun=ko\\
wife. 3poss=obj 3sg call= 3sg side= loc \\
`His wife he calls, she sits beside him.' [stim7_28:27]

Mujim=at in tok nawanggar\\
Mujim= obj 1pl.excl still wait\\
`For Mujim we're still waiting.' [narr1_1:21]

exe

Another way to topicalise a subject is by apposition of a more specific NP to a more general NP. This is done by apposing a pronoun and a noun, where the noun specifies the referent of the pronoun. There is no pause between the two NPs. ( exe:doubleA ) shows the apposition of esa main `his father' to the subject ma `he'. These constructions have been double-checked with two speakers to confirm that these are actual constructions and not repairs. In this example, the subject NPs are pronounced under one intonation contour.

exe

ma NP esa main NP afukat-sara\\
3sg father 3poss avocado-ascend\\
`He, his father climbed the avocado tree.' [stim34_0:16]

exe

In ( exe:doubleft ) there are even three juxtaposed NPs.

exe

ma NP tatanina opa NP ma NP buok kuru mia\\
3sg woman ana 3sg betel_nut bring come\\
`She, that woman, she came and brought betel nut just now.' [conv12_12:23]

exe

Anti-topics (AT) are constituents at the right edge of the clause, which serve to specify or reactivate a topic lambrecht1981. In ( exe:rd1 ), the subject of the clause, tumun opa me `that child', is specified in the postposed NP. It is also a reactivation of the topic, which had been mentioned a few turns earlier. Note that the anti-topic is also marked with anaphoric demonstrative opa and topic marker me. In ( exe:rd2 ), the object pesawat nunat `plane sounds', which was left out in the main clause, is mentioned in the postposed NP. Planes but not their sounds had been mentioned before in the narrative, so the specification at the end of the clause serves to indicate what people went to listen to.

exe

ma minggalot-un=ko tumun opa me AT \\
3sg bedroom- 3poss=loc child ana \\
`He's in his bed, that child.' [stim20_0:34]

mu utkon se bo keluan to pesawat nun=at AT \\
3pl some go listen right plane sound= obj \\
`Some went to listen, right, to the plane sounds.' [narr40_12:14]

exe
summary:
Topics are marked by reordering: a topicalized constituent may be fronted, optionally with the topic marker *me*, and if it is a subject or recipient in a give-construction it is repeated in the main clause; fronted objects are not repeated. A second way to topicalize a subject is by apposition of a pronoun and a more specific NP, with no pause between them.  

Anti-topics occur at the right edge of the clause and are used to specify or reactivate a topic. Focused constituents, by contrast, stay in their normal clause position and are marked with focus markers *=a* or *=ba*.

text:
predicate!complex|(

In Kalamang, complex predicates are monoclausal predicates with more than one verb or verb-like element with a shared argument. Verbs in complex predicates need not be contiguous: the verbs may be separated by an object object and an indirect object. They are of four morphosyntactic types, which are described in order of frequency: complex predicates connected by predicate linker =i (§ sec:mvci ), complex predicates with one dependent verb (§ sec:mvcdep ), complex source, goal and location predicates (§ sec:mvcgoal ) and serial verb constructions (§ sec:svc ). Serial verb constructions (SVCs) differ from the other types in that they are not linked by a predicate linker and that the verbs are independent That is, they can be the single predicate in a clause, and they can be inflected by all mood, aspect and modality markers available in Kalamang. This is a relatively minor type in Kalamang. Complex predicates are distinct from the clause-combining strategies described in § sec:clacomb.

All elements in complex predicates, being part of the same clause, have the same mood mood, aspect aspect and polarity polarity, which is only marked on the last verb. In other words, there can only be one instance of the same mood, aspect or modality marking per clause. An example of shared mood with the plural imperative is given in ( exe:jieborar ), contrasted with a biclausal example in ( exe:jierarku ). An example with a complex predicate with predicate linker =i is given in ( exe:cimei ).

exe

xlist
jie bo= tar \\
get go= pl.imp \\
`Go get!' [conv9_22:57]

jie= tar kuet= tar \\
get= pl.imp bring= pl.imp \\
`Get and bring!' [conv9_22:58]

xlist
mena ka nasuarik=i barei \\
later 2sg tuck= descend. imp \\
`Then you tuck [it] down!' [conv17_40:20]

exe

Also in non-contiguous predicates, mood, aspect and negation negation can only be expressed once. The imperative imperative marker in ( exe:yuatnar ) has scope over the entire predicate.

exe
melelu wele yuwa=at narari= te \\
sit vegetables prox=obj slice= imp \\
`Sit and slice these vegetables!' [elic_svc_33]

exe

Non-verbal predicates like NPs marked with a lative or locative postposition can also be part of complex predicates, as is shown by the prohibitive prohibitive enclitic =in on the locative pasierko `in the sea', which has scope over a predicate which also contains the verb gareor `to dump'.

an toni sor-kang me ki-mun gareor=i pasier=ko=in eh\\
1sg say fish-bone 2pl-proh dump= sea= loc=proh tag \\
`I said: ``Those fish bones, hey, don't you guys dump [them] in the sea!''' [conv10_14:05]

Shared aspect is illustrated here with progressive =teba. ( exe:mggt ) is a complex predicate; ( exe:mtggt ) contains two clauses with two predicates.

exe

xlist
emumur mambaran garung∼garung= teba \\
woman. pl stand chat∼ prog = \\
`The women stand chatting.' [elic_svc_37]

emumur mambara= teba garung∼garung= teba \\
woman. pl stand= chat∼ prog = \\
`The women are standing and [they] are chatting.' [elic_svc_39]

xlist
exe

-5ptFinally, consider an example of a negated predicate, where the negator is marked on the second verb masara `move towards land' in ( exe:kurumaratnin ).

exe
kalau mat kuru masarat=nin=et me pi barat=nin\\
if 3sg.obj bring move_landwards= neg = 1pl.incl descend= neg \\
`If [they] don't bring him towards land, we don't go down.' [conv7_4:22]

exe

Complex predicates with predicate linker =i

The most common type of complex predicate is made with predicate linker =i on all but the last word in the construction. They are monoclausal constructions with more than one independent verb or verb-like element and at least one shared argument. With the exception of `until'-constructions with bo `to go' (§ sec:mvcuntil ), no arguments can come between the elements in these predicates. I present different semantic types roughly in order of frequency of occurrence.

The use of predicate linker =i is ungrammatical with complex predicates with dependent verbs (§ sec:mvcdep ), directional verbs (§ sec:mvcgoal ) and bo `to go' (§ sec:svcbo ) as the first verb.

Aspectual serialisation with koyet `to be finished' aspect

Completive aspect, discussed in greater detail in § sec:compl, is made with help of the verb koyet `to be finished'. This is an independent verb, as illustrated in ( exe:kaitok ).

exe
kai tok koyet =nin\\
firewood yet finish= neg \\
`The firewood isn't finished yet.' [narr19_6:38]

exe

Completive aspect is expressed with the construction Verb =i koyet, where =i is attached to a matrix verb of any kind. At the same time as being a complex predicate, this construction sequentially links the state, event or action in the first clause (which has to be completed) to a state, event or action in the next clause (which was started after completion of the first). Multiple monoclausal Verb =i koyet constructions may be strung together in this way. There are no restrictions on the first verb in the predicate. Both verbs in the predicate share the same arguments. ( exe:ewunat ) shows the construction with a transitive verb in a narrative about making a canoe from a tree trunk. ( exe:yoriko ) is taken from the end of that narrative, and shows the construction on an intransitive verb. Although it is uncommon, even the verb koyet `to be finished' may be used as the matrix verb in this construction, as in ( exe:koyeri ).

exe
ewun=at potman= i koyet koi tim-un=at potma\\
stem= obj cut= finish then tip- 3poss=obj cut\\
`After cutting the stem, [I] cut its tips.' [narr42_0:17]

ma yor= i koyet... \\
3sg right= finish\\
`After it is right,....' [narr42_15:00]

koyet= i koyet kawarman\\
finish= finish fold\\
`After finishing, fold.' [narr11_2:29]

exe

It is also possible, though not often employed, to make aspectual serialisation with two verbs before koyet `to be finished', as in ( exe:tena ). There is not enough data to determine the relationship between the two verbs marked with =i.

exe
tena-un=at tawaran=i manyor=i koyet... \\
keel- 3poss=obj chop= adjust= finish... \\
`After chopping the keel straight,....' [narr42_3:01]

exe
summary:
Kalamang complex predicates are monoclausal constructions with more than one verb or verb-like element sharing an argument, and the elements may be non-contiguous. They come in four morphosyntactic types, with the most common using the predicate linker =i; serial verb constructions are a minor type and differ in being unlinked and fully independent, while complex predicates are distinct from clause-combining strategies.  

Across a complex predicate, mood, aspect, and negation are marked only once, usually on the final verb, so a single marker has scope over the whole predicate. The passage also illustrates aspectual serialization with koyet ‘be finished,’ where Verb =i koyet marks completive aspect and sequences the first event as completed before the next one begins.

text:
Lastly, aspectual serialisation is also used with locatives, which are NPs carrying locative postposition postposition!locative =ko functioning as predicates (§ sec:loc ).

exe
os=at di=timbang-un=ko=i koyet... \\
sand= obj caus =forehead- 3poss=loc = finish... \\
`After putting sand on her forehead,....' [conv8_3:02]

exe

Because this construction has a clause-linking function, it cannot be modified for other moods, aspects or modes. It cannot be negated. The construction also has related properties as a quantifier quantifier, meaning `all; until finished' (§ sec:quantall ). The relation between aspect and universal quantification is discussed for Timor-Alor languages in. See also: ``Completives differ from finish semantics in that the endpoint of the event is not reached by some actor wilfully ending it, but because a totality of referents is affected''. In § sec:compl, I argue that Kalamang =i koyet does both.
summary: Aspectual serialisation is also used with locative NPs marked by the locative postposition =ko, which function as predicates and link clauses. This construction cannot be negated or modified for other moods, aspects, or modes, and it has a related quantifier meaning of “all; until finished”; the author argues that Kalamang =i koyet combines this completive use with finish semantics.

text:
motion

Complex motion predicates have a motion verb as the second verb, and a manner or other verb as the first verb. The second verb is very commonly a directional verb (§ sec:dir ). The verbs share all arguments.

( exe:tumkar ) illustrates a manner and directional verb, ( exe:yalipa ) illustrates a manner and other motion verb, and ( exe:domanis ) shows the verb dorma `to pull out' with a directional verb.

exe
tumtum karuok marmar=i mia \\
children three walk= come\\
`Three children come walking.' [stim31_1:48]

setela ma yie=te an=a mat yal=i parei∼pareir \\
after 3sg swim= 1sg=foc 3sg.obj paddle= distr ∼follow\\
`After he [started] swimming I followed him paddling.' [narr44_1:28]

ar-un wa-rip ye dorman=i sara \\
stem- 3poss prox-qlt or pull_out= ascend\\
`Pull up [from the soil] a stem about as big as this.' [narr31_3:22]

exe

These constructions are also very common with (y)ecie `to return', making complex centrifugal motion constructions, as illustrated in ( exe:danik ).

exe
mat dan=i koyet se ecien=i sara \\
3sg.obj bury= finish return= ascend\\
`After burying him, [we] went back up.' [narr2_0:34]

exe

As with aspectual serialisation (§ sec:ikoyetsvc ), other complex predicates with predicate linker =i may also contain more than one verb. For example, in the manner + direction construction in ( exe:sirnag ), both manner verbs are marked with =i. Again, there is not enough data in the corpus to determine patterns in the (semantic) relationship between the verbs in the construction.

exe
nasirang=i mon∼mon=tun=i ran \\
pour= quick∼ ints=ints = go\\
`Go pour quickly.' [conv10_14:37]

exe

Nouns carrying -pis `side' (§ sec:inal ) are also inflected with =i when they modify a verb.

exe
kon se marmar=i talep-pis=i bot \\
one walk= outside-side= go\\
`One is walking outside.' [stim14_2:33]

exe

This is also the case for NPs carrying similative postposition postposition!similative =kap, like ododa `gado-gado' (a dish) in ( exe:ododang ). Most colour terms end in -gap or -kap and are probably derived from nouns marked with similative =kap (§ sec:sim ), but are treated as monomorphemic. They can also be inflected with =i and become part of a complex predicate, like baranggap `yellow' in ( exe:gawi ).

exe
ododa=kap=i paruot=et\\
gado_gado= sim = make= \\
`Make [it] like gado-gado.' [conv15_5:20]

wa me paden taikon baranggap=i saran \\
prox pole one_side yellow= ascend\\
`This one, a yellow pole goes down on one side.' [stim39_1:27]

exe

Three manner adverbials, described in § sec:manner, end in /i/, but it is not clear at this point whether this is predicate linker =i.
summary:
Complex motion predicates consist of a motion verb in second position, preceded by a manner verb or another verb, and the two verbs share all their arguments. The second verb is often a directional verb, and similar constructions are common with *yecie* ‘return’ to form centrifugal motion; the passage also notes that other predicates with linker *=i* can contain multiple verbs, but the corpus does not yet show clear semantic patterns among them.  

Items such as nouns with *-pis* ‘side’ and NPs with the similative postposition *=kap* can also take *=i* when modifying a verb and participate in complex predicates; some colour terms ending in *-gap/-kap* may historically come from similative forms, though they are treated as monomorphemic.

text:
Complex action and result predicates express an action in the first verb and a result in the second verb. Like resultative SVCs, § sec:ressvc, they are rare. One natural spoken corpus example is ( exe:kakat ) with the verbs komain `to stab' and rua `to kill'. The object of the first verb is the subject of the second, such that the verbs in the construction do not share any arguments. In ( exe:dakcamp ), it is unclear exactly whether campur `to mix' is the result obtained by chopping two ingredients and the same time, or whether this should be read as two sequential events. The same conversation also contains the construction kawareni campur `grate mix'.

exe
o mu se kaka=at komain=i rua \\
int 3pl older_sibling= obj stab= kill\\
`O, they killed the older brother (by stabbing).' [narr24_3:51]

mier-gan=at paruo dakdak=i campur \\
3du -all= obj make chop= mix\\
`Mix both of them (by chopping).' [conv20_13:24]

exe

A few other examples of action-result constructions with predicate linker =i were elicited with help of the cut and break clips cutbreak2001. Here, the resultative function of the constructions is clear. Consider ( exe:donsl ) and ( exe:pueip ).

exe
ma karek=at ramien=i meraraouk \\
3sg string= obj pull= cause_to_snap\\
`He causes the string to snap (by pulling it).' [elic_cut_28]

pue=i parair\\
hit= break\\
`[Of a clip where a pot is smashed with a hammer:] break (by hitting).' [elic_cut_39]

exe
summary: Complex action and result predicates describe an action in the first verb and the resulting state in the second, and they are rare, like resultative serial verb constructions. In the corpus examples, the first verb’s object becomes the subject of the second verb, so the two verbs do not share arguments; some cases clearly express a result, while others could also be interpreted as two sequential events. Elicited examples with the linker =i more clearly show resultative meanings, such as causing a string to snap by pulling it or breaking something by hitting it.

text:
durative until

Reduplicated verbs marked with predicate linker =i occur in two contexts. The first is with reduplicated verbs that indicate durativity, followed by a construction with `until' which indicates the result of the action. The `until'-construction (with help of bo `to go') may (example exe:kadok ) or may not (example exe:kuarkuar ) be made in a separate clause. The second is in constructions with verbs that indicate durativity, but without an explicitly linked action (example exe:rawiraw ), or with an implied `until'-construction (example exe:komainik ). The verbs are typically lengthened (§ sec:lenght ), as indicated in ( exe:rawiraw ).

exe
kit-kadok=at paruon=i paruon=i bo koyet\\
top-side= obj make= make= go finish\\
`[We] made the top-side until [it was] finished.' [narr7_2:45]

kuar=i kuar=i ma se bo ruon\\
cook= cook= 3sg go cooked\\
`Cooking, cooking, until it's cooked.' [narr8_2:10]

mier se mu=at komain=i komain=i kon se tur\\
3du 3pl=obj stab= stab= one fall\\
`They stabbed and stabbed [until] one fell.' [narr28_9:10]

inier se melalu raːwi raːwi \\
inier se melelu rap=i rap=i\\
1du.ex sit laugh= laugh= \\
`We sat laughing, laughing.' [narr44_22:46]

exe

The `until'-constructions with bo `to go' illustrated in ( exe:kadok ) and ( exe:kuarkuar ) are also often found with distal manner demonstrative!manner demonstrative mindi and another verb, marked with predicate linker =i. The order is Verb= plnk + `like that' + `go' (example exe:karuarr ). The construction can be elaborated with mendak, a demonstrative form probably derived from distal demonstrative me and clitic =tak `just', meaning `just like that' (§ sec:distmann ). The `until'-construction then takes the form mendak=i + mindi + bo (example exe:nasuis ). See § sec:distmann for a discussion of the uses of the distal manner demonstrative mindi.

exe
karuar=i mindi bo kararak koi masan\\
smoke_dry= like_that go dry then dry_in_sun\\
`We dry [on a rack above the fire] until it's dry, then we dry in the sun.' [narr11_2:50]

mu ko=melelu mendak=i mindi bo ma se nasuk=i saran\\
3pl appl =sit just_like_that= like_that go 3sg go_backwards= ascend\\
`They sit on it until it [the haemorrhoids] has gone back up.' [narr36_0:53]

exe

The corpus also includes `until'-constructions with Austronesian loans like sampe `until' or selama `as long as' preceded by a verb marked with predicate linker =i.
summary:
Reduplicated verbs marked with predicate linker =i occur in two main uses: either with a following `until'-construction that expresses the result of the action, or by themselves to indicate durative action with an implied `until' meaning. In these constructions, the `until' clause may be separate or combined with the verb `go' (bo), and the verbs are often lengthened.

The passage also notes a related pattern with distal manner demonstratives like mindi, sometimes elaborated with mendak, and says that the corpus includes `until'-constructions using Austronesian loans such as sampe `until' and selama `as long as'.

text:
give-construction

Give-constructions (§ sec:give ) are made with a zero morpheme `give'. They may and frequently do occur without any other verb in the clause. However, they also occur in complex predicates with predicate linker =i. The verb marked with =i precedes the recipient. The zero morpheme `give' comes after the recipient, which makes these discontinuous complex predicates. The verbs only share their subject, and the recipient comes between the two verbs. The theme (pandanus leaf in the first example and fish in the second) is the direct object of both verbs.

exe
naman=a padanual=at rep=i ka ∅\\
who= foc pandanus= obj get= 2sg give\\
`Who got pandanus [leaf] and gave it to you?' [conv17_23:37]

an toni kuru ma yap=i sontum=ki ∅\\
1sg say bring move_landwards divide= person= ben give\\
`I said bring it here and divide it among people.' [conv19_8:42]

exe

Like with other types of complex predicates with predicate linker =i, we also find multiple verbs marked with =i in give-constructions. Consider ( exe:ningetmet ). As for the other types, there is not enough data to systematically analyse the relationship among the =i -marked verbs.

summary: Give-constructions are formed with a zero morpheme meaning ‘give’ and can occur either alone or in complex predicates with the linker =i. In these complex predicates, the =i-marked verb precedes the recipient, while the zero ‘give’ follows it, creating a discontinuous structure in which the two verbs share only the subject and the theme functions as the direct object of both verbs. The text also notes that multiple verbs can be marked with =i in give-constructions, though there is not enough data to analyze their relationship systematically.

text:
dependent verb

All four Kalamang dependent verbs occur in complex predicates. These verbs cannot be negated or inflected for e.g. aspectual and modal categories. Two of the dependent verbs ( kuru `bring' and bon `bring') occur as the first verb in the construction, and one ( eranun `cannot; not be possible') occurs as the second verb in the construction. Toni can occur in both positions. As the first verb, it means `want', and as the second verb, it means `say' or `think'.

With kuru `bring'

The independent verb kuet `to bring', illustrated in ( exe:mingkuet ), is only rarely combined with other verbs into a complex predicate, and is then always marked with predicate linker =i, as in ( exe:kueri ). It is also used in give-constructions, which have the zero morpheme `give', as in ( exe:kuerima ).

exe

2sg grandmother oil- 3poss prox=obj bring= \\
`You bring this oil of granny.' [conv12_2:21]

little first bring= move\\
`First bring over that little bit.' [conv9_9:41]

bring= 3sg give\\
`Bring him.' [elic_i19_4]

exe

However, there is a dependent verb kuru `bring' which occurs as the first verb in complex predicates expressing transfer and motion. Kuru `bring' cannot be used independently, and never carries any morphology. The most common construction is with a directional verb (§ sec:dir ), illustrated in ( exe:adiun ), or another verb expressing motion, such as luk `come' in ( exe:kurluk ).

`He came towards land and [he] brought his brother towards sea.' [narr28_12:46]

See § sec:svcloclat for more complex predicates expressing source, goal or location.

With bon `bring'

The dependent verb bon `bring' (possibly related to comitative postposition postposition!comitative =bon, § sec:comi ) occurs as the first verb in a complex predicate in combination with a motion verb like tiri `to run' (example exe:borus ), rep `to get', marmar `to walk', bo `to go', bara `to descend' (example exe:bonbara ) or sara `to ascend'.

`That child goes up the deer's antlers, he brings him running.' [stim20_4:43]

`Desi came down carrying [the child], bringing it down from there.' [conv11_5:50]

While kuru `bring' is a generic bring-verb, bon `bring' can only be used for things that are carried by the subject (and not, for example, escorted).

With toni `say; think; want'

The dependent verb toni `say; think; want' is used with the meaning `say; think' as the second verb in complex predicates in combination with verbs expressing speech, thought, or sensation, such as taruo `to say', as illustrated in ( exe:ttoni ). Other verbs accompanied by toni are gerket `to ask', narasa `to feel' and konawaruo `to forget'. More examples are given in § sec:speech.

exe

exe

With the meaning `want' (discussed in detail in § sec:kin ), toni can be the first verb in a complex predicate, without any restriction on the semantics of the other verb. An example with bara `to descend' is given in ( exe:tonibara ). It is unclear whether toni `want' can be used without volitional =kin (§ sec:kin ). The corpus instances of toni followed by a verb that is not marked with =kin are ambiguous between the `want' and the `say; think' reading.

exe

eagle want descend 3sg.obj grab= vol \\
`The eagle wants to descend and grab him.' [stim20_4:21]

exe

With eranun `cannot'
The dedicated negative verb eranun `cannot; to not be possible' is not a full verb: it cannot be inflected for mood and aspect. Moreover, it must always be preceded by another verb. This verb is nominalised with -un, such as karajang `to work' in ( exe:noobody ). For a further discussion of this construction, see § sec:lexicalneg.

som kon- barak karajang-un eranun \\
person one-any work- nmlz cannot\\
`No-one can do the work.' [elic_ind]
summary: Kalamang has four dependent verbs that occur only in complex predicates and cannot be negated or inflected for categories such as aspect or mood. The passage describes their functions: **kuru** and **bon** mean ‘bring’ in different kinds of transfer/motion constructions, **toni** means either ‘say/think’ as a second verb or ‘want’ as a first verb, and **eranun** is a negative verb meaning ‘cannot’ that must follow another verb.

section: Complex source, goal and location predicates
text:
location

Complex source, goal and location constructions can be made with locative and lative postpositions, § sec:svcloclat, or with causative causative di=, § sec:svcdi. They are made by means of the different complex predicates presented in this section, and show a variety of order constraints.
summary: Complex source, goal, and location constructions can be formed with locative and lative postpositions or with the causative **di=**. They are built using the different complex predicates discussed in this section, and these constructions exhibit a range of ordering restrictions.

section: Complex source, goal and location predicates
text:
postposition!locative postposition!lative

Source, goal and location are commonly expressed with help of four postpositions: locative =ko, animate locative =konggo, lative =ka and animate lative =kongga (§ sec:loc, § sec:lat and § sec:animloclat ). While a NP marked with a locative postposition may and frequently does occur as the predicate of the clause, without any other verb, a NP marked with a lative postposition must be followed by a verb. In both cases, these locative and lative constructions may combine with other verbs to create even more complex goal, source and location predicates. The options for these complex predicates are given in Table tab:loclatsvc. The building blocks of these predicates are three groups of verbs: manner verbs, verbs expressing motion and other verbs. These combine in a limited number of ways with NPs carrying a locative or lative clitic. Six slots in these complex predicates can be distinguished: three before and two after the noun with the postposition. The first slot is reserved for manner verbs (marked with predicate linker =i, § sec:mvci ) and kuru `to bring' (§ sec:mvckuru ). Motion verbs occur in either the second or the fifth slot. Motion verbs include all verbs expressing motion: the directional verbs (§ sec:dir ), bo `to go' (§ sec:svcbo ) and other verbs like taluk `to come out'. In some constructions, only bo `to go' is allowed in the motion slot; in others, bo `to go' is specifically not allowed in the motion slot. In one case, only motion verbs that are not bo or a directional are allowed. Bo `to go' has its own slot before the NP with the postposition. The verb slot (V), finally, is normally used for any verb, including the aforementioned. In one construction, this slot is used for a directional verb. In all cases, if bo `to go' precedes the locative or lative, it takes the form bo. If it follows it, it takes the form bot (see also § sec:svcbo ).

While all constructions have several examples in the natural spoken corpus, not all are found (or tested) with the animate forms =konggo and =kongga, which are much less frequent in the corpus. There is, however, no reason to assume they would behave differently. More constructions may be found if more data become available. Each type will be exemplified in turn below. The standard locative construction is described in § sec:loc and the standard lative construction is described in § sec:lat.

The four complex predicates where one or more verbs precede the locative are all goal constructions, i.e. expressing movement towards a goal. This order obeys the principle of iconicity: the goal, the endpoint of the movement, follows the motion verb. The fifth complex predicate in the table, which has verbs preceding and following the locative, expresses both movement towards a goal and the posture taken at the location of the goal.
The last complex locative predicate in the table, where a verb follows the locative, is a static locative construction. In ( exe:weleop ), the locative is combined with waruo `to wash', but the verb is also often a posture verb like maraouk `to put', mambara `to stand' or melelu `to sit' (cf. posture SVCs in § sec:post ).

All latives must be followed by a verb, regardless of the construction. Most constructions can express both movement from a source and movement towards a goal. These constructions are not iconic, so the correct reading must always be inferred from the context. The construction manner + bo + lative + Verb is rare: there are only two examples in the corpus, both of which express movement towards a goal.
summary:
The passage explains that source, goal, and location are expressed with four postpositions: locative and animate locative, and lative and animate lative. A locative NP can function as the clause predicate by itself, but a lative NP must always be followed by a verb; these constructions can also combine with manner, motion, and other verbs in a limited set of slot-based patterns.

It further notes that locative constructions with verbs before the postposition are goal constructions, ordered iconically so that the endpoint follows the motion verb, while a verb after the locative yields a static locative reading. Lative constructions are less iconic and can express either source or goal depending on context, with one rare pattern attested only for goal motion.

section: Complex source, goal and location predicates
text:
causative

Causative di= (§ sec:di ) occurs in combination with directional verbs and locations in complex causative predicates. It attaches to the left edge of the complex predicate. It is also optionally employed in give-constructions (§ sec:give ). ( exe:bint ) is an example of a complex causative predicate with ra `to move (away); to become' (§ sec:svcra ).

exe
mendak embir-ne=ka sasul di=ra bintang ne= ko \\
like_that bucket-inside= lat spoon caus =move tub inside= loc \\
`So [I] spooned from the bucket into a tub.' [conv13_3:11]

exe
summary: Causative **di=** appears with directional verbs and locations in complex causative predicates, and it attaches to the left edge of the complex predicate. It is also optionally used in **give-constructions**. The example with **ra** ‘move away; become’ shows a causative meaning of moving something from one location into another.

text:
serial verb construction

Following and, I define serial verb constructions (SVCs) as monoclausal constructions with more than one independent verb, no linking element between the verbs, and with at least one shared argument. This is a morphosyntactic definition for a morphosyntactic phenomenon. Often-used criteria such as intonation and event structure (in e.g. ) are argued to be hard to falsify and to follow from a morphosyntactic definition (e.g. ). This type of complex predicate is not very common in Kalamang. SVCs can be divided into symmetrical SVCs (with verbs from open verb classes, § sec:symsvc ) and asymmetrical SVCs (with at least one verb from a restricted class, § sec:asymsvc ).
summary: Serial verb constructions are defined here as monoclausal structures containing more than one independent verb, no linker between the verbs, and at least one shared argument. The passage notes that this is a morphosyntactic definition, and that other criteria such as intonation and event structure are considered difficult to falsify and likely to follow from this definition. In Kalamang, serial verb constructions are not very common and are divided into symmetrical SVCs, with verbs from open classes, and asymmetrical SVCs, with at least one verb from a restricted class.

text:
serial verb construction!symmetrical

Symmetrical SVCs consist of verbs from open verb classes, with no restrictions on the semantics of the verb. All components in a symmetrical SVC contribute equally to its meaning, so there is no `head' in the construction. Symmetrical SVCs express events consisting of two or more active verbs, given in sequential order (obeying the iconicity of order, [29]staden2008). They share their arguments. ( exe:jieborar ) above is a symmetrical SVC. Additional examples are provided in ( exe:potmapar ) to ( exe:kajkow ). Note that in ( exe:perjiena ), the noun is incorporated into the SVC (see § sec:incorp on noun incorporation) noun incorporation.

exe
pawan=at worman=i koyet in koi potman=i koyet timun=at potma paruak \\
plank= obj cut_down= finish 1pl.excl then cut= finish tip= obj cut drop\\
`After cutting down [trees for] planks, after cutting, [we] cut off the tips.' [narr14_5:00]

in=a per-jie na \\
1pl.excl=foc water-get consume\\
`We fetched water and drank.' [narr40_1:45]

usar=et mul-un=ka kajien kowarman \\
erect= side- 3poss = lat pick fold\\
`Erect [the basket], pick and fold [strips] from the side.' [narr11_0:38]

exe

When an unmarked directional verb (§ sec:dir ) is in the first position of a complex predicate, the construction can be a SVC. Like the examples above, they are sequential actions with a shared subject. They can also be purposive, such as bara komet `come down to look' in ( exe:barakom ). If a directional verb in a complex predicate is preceded by a non-directional verb, this verb is always marked with =i (described in § sec:mvci ), and this construction is thus not a SVC. ( exe:marabara ) and ( exe:ranmina ) show SVCs of two directional verbs. ( exe:ragerket ), finally, shows a SVC with shared subject, separated by the object of the second verb.

summary: Symmetrical serial verb constructions (SVCs) are made up of verbs from open classes with no semantic restrictions, and all verbs contribute equally to the meaning, so there is no head. They describe sequential actions with shared arguments, often following the iconic order of events; examples include constructions with incorporated nouns and with unmarked directional verbs in initial position, which may also express purposive meanings. If a directional verb follows a non-directional verb, it is marked with =i and the result is not an SVC, while some SVCs may contain two directional verbs or have the object of the second verb intervening between shared-subject verbs.

text:
serial verb construction!asymmetrical

Asymmetrical SVCs have one or more verbs from a restricted class of verbs. In most cases described here, this is not a syntactic subclass of verbs; rather, one of the verbs is from a particular semantic class. Some asymmetrical verb constructions may only occur with one particular verb. All asymmetrical SVCs have a fixed order, where the verb from the (most) restricted class usually is the first verb.

With bo `go'

The single most common asymmetrical SVC is with bo `to go', an independent verb that can be modified with all mood, aspect and modality markers available in Kalamang. It is, however, also an irregular verb, which always takes the form bot when it is the only verb in the construction, but bo when it occurs in a SVC (see § sec:stems for an introduction to verb roots in -t, and § sec:ntverbs for a discussion of these as a separate verb class). Alternatively, it could be argued that bo is an independent form of bot. In that case, complex predicates with bo are not SVCs. It is multifunctional, and always occurs as the first verb in the SVC.

First, it occurs in purposive motion serialisation, where bo `to go' indicates the movement of the subject, and the second verb indicates the purpose. The second verb can be any dynamic verb, transitive or intransitive. Consider the following examples with an intransitive verb, a transitive verb with incorporated object, and a transitive verb with object, respectively.

exe
ma toni e an bo war=kin \\
3sg say int 1sg go fish= vol \\
`He said: ``Eh, I go fishing.''' [conv10_13:26]

`One of the children went to collect firewood.' [narr23_5:21]

3pl first go coconut_leaf= obj ascend\\
`They first went to harvest [lit. ascend] coconut leaves.' [narr3_10:54]

exe

Second, bo `to go' occurs in SVCs with stative intransitive verbs in change-of-state serialisation. Like in purposive motion serialisation, bo `to go' needs to be the first verb in the construction. Consider ( exe:borei ) and ( exe:eiririr ).

`We became many people, like that.' [conv7_12:38]

A fixed expression that is a variant of change-of-state serialisation with bo `to go' and tik `to take a long time' is bo tik `before long'. Note that change-of-state can also be expressed with nominals referring to times of the day in predicate function, e.g. bo go saun `until the evening; after it had turned evening' (with go saun `evening' ).

Third, bo `to go' occurs in constructions with locatives and latives to indicate motion towards a goal (see § sec:svcloclat ).

With ra `move'

Purposive motion serialisation can also be achieved with the directional verb ra `to move (along a path); to become' as V1. It is less generic than bo `to go', described above, in that it specifies the path of motion in combination with the other verb. This is also evident from its use as the antonym of mia `to come' (as in exe:ranmina above). In ( exe:mast ), the use of ra refers to the path from a floating fish cage to a boat. In ( exe:kulp ), the path from the speaker to the fire is indicated by ra. ( exe:pasaromat ) is made with ra and the zero morpheme `give', to indicate the path between the giver and the recipient.

Ra `to move' is also used as the second verb in constructions with dependent verb kuru `to bring' (§ sec:mvckuru, example exe:kwarin ), as the second verb in complex predicates linked by predicate linker =i (§ sec:mvci, example exe:sirnag ), and in causative constructions (§ sec:svcdi, example exe:bint ).

With melelu `sit' and mambara `stand' posture

SVCs with melelu `to sit' and mambara `to stand' (introduced in examples exe:mggt and exe:mtggt above) can tentatively be grouped as posture SVCs. The first verb in the construction is the posture verb, and the second is a transitive or intransitive verb expressing some kind of activity. The verbs share the same subject.

With bara `descend' resultative

There is one example of an asymmetrical SVC that is composed of an activity and a result, and that may tentatively be termed resultative. It consists of the directional verb bara `to descend' and the stative intransitive verb stative intransitive verb pol `to be compact'. They share the same subject: soil. The context is digging soil for making the foundation of a house. The speaker says that one shouldn't use soil without small stones, because otherwise, if it rains, the soil will become too compact.

summary: Asymmetrical serial verb constructions in Kalamang have one or more verbs from a restricted class, usually determined by semantics rather than by a special syntactic verb class, and they occur in a fixed order with the restricted verb typically first. The passage describes several types: purposive motion with **bo** ‘go’, path-related purposive motion with **ra** ‘move’, posture constructions with **melelu** ‘sit’ and **mambara** ‘stand’, a resultative example with **bara** ‘descend’, and a causative type with **paruo** ‘make, do’.

text: Clausal modifiers in Kalamang are words, a single particle, proclitics, enclitics and suffixes that modify the predicate or clause in one of the following ways. They can change the mood, aspect or mode of a predicate or clause, or specify the manner, temporal setting, degree or other characteristics of the state or event expressed by the predicate, such as repetition repetition or exclusivity.
summary: Clausal modifiers in Kalamang include words, a single particle, proclitics, enclitics, and suffixes that modify the predicate or clause. They can alter mood, aspect, or mode, or specify features such as manner, temporal setting, degree, repetition, exclusivity, and other characteristics of the state or event expressed by the predicate.

text:
Table tab:modifiersall provides an overview of the different kinds of clausal modifiers, as well as their slot in the clause and where in the chapter they are described. Negation is described in § sec:clauneg. Clausal modifiers are structurally very diverse: they can be words, clitics on the predicate, suffixes on the pronoun, or a particle auxiliary*, so they are described according to function from § sec:TAM onwards. passive*|seeclausal modification evidential*|seeclausal modification mirative*|seeclausal modification clausal modification

There is one slot before the subject, three slots between the subject and the object, two between object and predicate, and three after the predicate. Modifiers that occupy the same slot are mutually exclusive, with the exception of slots 6 and 7, where the waters are a bit murky (see comments below). Some slots (2, 6, 7) are not for words, but for dependent morphology only. The template for clausal modification is given in ( exe:tamplate ).

It is impossible to capture all the details of predicate and clausal modification in the table, so please note the following things. First, several modifiers can occur in more than one slot. This is the case for modal markers bisa `can' and harus `must'. Bisa `can', moreover, can also be the predicate itself, and inflect for irrealis =et. Second, some modifiers are discontinuous and occur in several slots at the same time. The prohibitive is formed by simultaneously placing suffix -mun on the subject and clitic =in on the predicate. Modal marker suka - poss `not like; not want' must either be combined with a negated verb, or can be the predicate itself if followed by propositional negator ge. The position of negator =nin is indicated in the table. Negation is described in § sec:clauneg. Third, the use of modal marker eranun `cannot' turns the preceding predicate into a noun. Fourth, some of the predicate enclitics in 6 and 7 can co-occur, while cannot. Completive =i koyet and intensifier =tun may be followed by irrealis =et. Volitional =kin (as well as negator =nin ) can be followed by progressive =teba and irrealis =et. Progressive =teba, in turn, may also be followed by irrealis =et and is therefore listed in both slots 6 and 7. Fifth, the placement of modal markers in slot 3 relative to the aspectual particle se and word tok, also given in slot 3, is not entirely clear. More data are needed to see if it is appropriate to posit another slot between current 2 and 3.

The next part of this chapter outlines the particularities of all predicate and clausal modifiers, starting with mood, aspect and modality marking (§ sec:TAM ), followed by the different adverbial modifiers in § sec:adv.
summary: The passage explains that clausal modifiers in the language are structurally diverse, including words, clitics, suffixes, and auxiliary particles, and are described functionally rather than by form. It presents a clause template with fixed slots around the subject, object, and predicate, notes that modifiers in the same slot are generally mutually exclusive, and highlights several complications such as modifiers appearing in multiple slots, discontinuous forms, uncertain slot distinctions, and some predicate enclitics that can co-occur.

text: Mood, aspect and modality markers are clausal modifiers indicating the speakers' attitudes towards what they are saying, or the internal temporal constituency of a state or event. Most of these are clitics that attach to the predicate, one is a particle, and some (namely modal markers) are independent words. Because they are structurally so diverse, they are described by function. I describe irrealis mood (§ sec:et ), volitional mood (§ sec:kin ), the imperative and prohibitive moods (§ sec:imp ), aspectual markers iamitive se and tok `still; yet; first' (§ sec:setok ), progressive aspect (§ sec:teba ), completive aspect (§ sec:compl ) and modal markers (§ sec:modal ). Kalamang has no tense tense* marking. One modal and one mood marker are described elsewhere: the modal apprehensive marker -re and other strategies to form apprehensive constructions are described in § sec:appreh, and conditional mood marker =o / =ero and other strategies for making conditional clauses are described in § sec:condclause.
summary: The passage explains that Kalamang uses mood, aspect, and modality markers as clausal modifiers expressing speakers’ attitudes or the internal temporal structure of events. These markers are structurally varied—mostly clitics, plus one particle and some independent modal words—so they are organized by function, and the language has no tense marking. It then lists the main categories discussed in the grammar and notes that the apprehensive and conditional markers are treated elsewhere.

text:
mood|(
Mood markers indicate the speaker's attitude towards the event or condition in their utterance. Kalamang morphologically marks irrealis, volitional, imperative, prohibitive, conditional and apprehensive mood by means of enclitics on the predicate and/or suffixes on the subject. Mood markers are found in slot 2 (on the subject) and slots 6 and 7 (attaching to the predicate).

Irrealis =et ` irr ' irrealis

Irrealis mood is marked by enclitic =et on the predicate. This is a very versatile mood, used in all kinds of hypothetical or prospective situations. It has not been investigated exactly which semantic categories are (not) encoded with irrealis =et, and whether irrealis marking is obligatory for any or all of these.

( exe:seteba ) and ( exe:diwatkok ) are taken from a recording where two women sit with different kinds of fishing gear and explain how they (would) use it. In ( exe:sortam ), someone asks what they should do with their newly caught fish. ( exe:rumasa ) expresses a command and a possible result or consequence. Irrealis =et comes at the end of a breath group.

Volitional =kin ` vol ' volitional

Volitional mood enclitic =kin attaches to the predicate. It is mainly used to express plans and wishes, as well as events that are about to happen. The different uses of =kin are exemplified in ( exe:kin ) to ( exe:kin2 ). ( exe:kin ) expresses a plan or wish. In ( exe:kintoni ), the common use of =kin with toni `want' is illustrated. It is unclear whether toni `want' can be used without volitional =kin. Toni can also mean `say; think' (§ sec:mvctoni ), so many of the corpus instances of toni followed by a verb that is not marked with =kin are ambiguous between the `want' and the `say; think' reading. The phrase in ( exe:kinabout ) is used to describe the twelfth picture in the Family problems picture task carroll2009, where a child is falling out of its mother's arms, and illustrates the prospective use of =kin. ( exe:kin2 ) is the first utterance in a text where a woman explains how to make a basket. It can be interpreted as an action that is about to happen (at least in the speaker's mind) or as a plan. prospective irrealis mood volitional

summary: Kalamang marks several moods with enclitics and subject suffixes, including irrealis, volitional, imperative, prohibitive, conditional, and apprehensive. Irrealis =et attaches to the predicate and is used in hypothetical, prospective, conditional, and some sequential contexts, while volitional =kin also attaches to the predicate and expresses plans, wishes, and imminent events; when used conditionally, =kin precedes =et.

Imperative =te ` imp ' imperative

Imperative mood, used for commands, is formed by adding =te (singular, though occasionally used for plural) or =tar (plural plural!verbal ) to the predicate. The subject may be elided. ( exe:meieba ) shows the singular imperative cliticised to the verb kome `look', and ( exe:metkore ) shows it cliticised to the locative demonstrative metko `there', which functions as the predicate in that clause. Of the locative predicates that are marked with the imperative, it only occurs on those locative predicates that express movement towards a goal, not on locatives that express static location location (§ sec:loc ). The plural imperative person marking indexing|seeperson marking is illustrated in ( exe:borar ). Imperative =te follows aspectual marker =teba, as in ( exe:tebare ).

Directional verbs (which end in -a ) and transitive verbs ending in -ma, described in § sec:dir and § sec:macie, have imperative forms where final -a is replaced with -ei. For example, bara `go down' has the imperative form barei (example exe:barei ) and potma has the imperative form potmei (example exe:potmei ). These are also both examples of predicate!complex complex predicates, which show that the imperative is marked on the second verb, and has scope over the whole construction. An exception is the imperative of mia, which becomes not miei but mei, as in ( exe:meieba ) above.

Prohibitive =in ` proh ' prohibitive

Prohibitive mood is expressed with a dedicated construction involving suffix -mun on the pronominal subject and clitic =in on the predicate. ( exe:ewain2 ) shows a clause in prohibitive mood with =in on a verbal predicate, and ( exe:koineh ) shows =in on a locative predicate. There is no distinct plural form of the prohibitive. The combination of -mun and negator =nin is ungrammatical. Alternatively, one could say that prohibitive =in triggers the use of special prohibitive pronoun forms (since the form -mun only occurs on pronouns).

Like in the imperative mood, prohibitive forms of directional verbs and transitive verbs in -ma are different: instead of ending in -a + -in, they become -ein. ( exe:mumun ) illustrates a prohibitive with a third person plural.

Most clausal modifiers are incompatible with the prohibitive. The aspectual particle se `already' (iamitive) and the aspectual word tok `yet; still; first' ( nondum nondum), however, are compatible. The combination of the iamitive se and the prohibitive results in the meaning `not anymore' (i.e. the iamitive has scope over the prohibitive). The nondum tok plus a prohibitive results in the meaning `not yet', illustrated in ( exe:muntok2 ). This is parallel to the meanings of the iamitive and nondum with regular verbal negation negation, as illustrated in Table tab:setok in § sec:setok.

summary:
The passage describes how imperatives are formed with the clitics =te for singular and =tar for plural, attached to the predicate, with the subject often omitted. It also notes special imperative forms for directional and some transitive verbs, where final -a becomes -ei, and that the plural form for many -n/-t verbs is likely =r.  

For prohibitives, the language uses a dedicated construction with -mun on the pronominal subject and =in on the predicate; there is no separate plural prohibitive, and -mun cannot attach directly to nouns. The passage further states that some clausal modifiers are normally incompatible with prohibitives, though se ‘already’ and tok ‘yet/still/first’ can combine with them to yield meanings like ‘not anymore’ and ‘not yet’.

General prohibition, not directed at a specific person, is expressed with ka-mun or ki-mun, second-person singular or plural, respectively. One could use this, for example, on a prohibition sign. In spoken Kalamang, one may also leave out the verb, and just use the second person ka-mun! `don't!'.

Conditional =o/=ero ` cond ' conditional|(

Conditional mood is made with conditional clitic =o or =ero, which attaches to the predicate with the condition. The condition is followed by a new clause with the consequence. It occurs about ten times in the corpus, and mostly in contexts with several conditions. The two variants of the clitic are given in ( exe:warobes ) and ( exe:geroo ). ( exe:geroo ) also shows a negative condition. ( exe:nanere ) shows a possible third variant, =ere, but it occurs only in that utterance. Note that the consequence is expressed as just a predicate in all cases in the corpus. There is not enough data to determine for which types of conditions (e.g. implicative, predictive, indicative, counterfactual) these clitics are used.

A variant on the conditional is =taero `even if', which is a concessive that indicates that the condition in the first clause does not prevent the statement in the second clause from being true. Like =ero, =taero `even if' attaches to the condition, i.e. the predicate of the first clause, which is followed by a predicate-only clause with the consequence. The clitic is frequently combined with Malay loan biar `even if', which precedes the conditional clause, without a change in meaning.

Apprehensive =re ` appr ' apprehensive

Apprehensive mood, used when the speaker wishes to express fear that something bad will happen, is done with an apprehensive clitic =re, which is attached to the subject or object NP of the clause. The predicate is marked with irrealis =et (§ sec:et ), and many clauses are preceded by the interjection interjection jaga `watch out' (a Malay loan). In contrast to precautionary constructions (§ sec:appreh ), only the danger is expressed and not necessarily the precaution to be taken. This morpheme is not found in the natural speech corpus, but was easily elicited with the help of pictures designed by Marine Vuillermet (p.c.) depicting dangerous situations, or by simply asking speakers what they would say in a specific dangerous situation. Examples of pictures were that of a snake under a chair (example exe:kipkader ), or a crocodile approaching a human being. An example of a dangerous situation I described is walking on the beach under palm trees bearing ripe coconuts. In that situation, someone might utter ( exe:watre ). Note that in this example, the suggested precaution to take is also expressed in an imperative clause preceding the apprehensive clause.

In the previous examples, the apprehensive morpheme =re is attached to the noun that refers to the danger. In intransitive clauses, the danger is the addressee themselves, because they are behaving irresponsibly. In ( exe:kire ), the speaker utters an imaginary warning to kids jumping from the dock. If they do not jump far enough away from a dock, they might hit sharp rocks.

summary:
The passage describes several moods in Kalamang. Prohibitive =in attaches to the last constituent of a predicate complex and scopes over the whole construction, while general prohibitions use ka-mun or ki-mun, sometimes with no verb at all; conditional mood uses =o/=ero, with a variant =taero meaning “even if,” and these clitics attach to the condition clause whose consequence is a predicate-only clause. 

It also discusses the apprehensive mood, marked by =re on the subject or object NP and combined with irrealis =et on the predicate, often preceded by jaga ‘watch out.’ This mood expresses fear that a bad event may occur, and intransitive examples show the danger as involving the addressee themselves.
